div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS,

A GENTLEMAN went up to an apple stall, and asked the old woman if the apples were sweet. With a wise wag of her head, she replied— " Warranted, sir—st den l" NOBODY but a loving mother could weep bitter tears over a lost child, and then spank it ener- getical:y for returning, MRS. WITHERBY : "What did your cook do? Go off in a huff 1" Mrs. Piankington : "No. She went off in my tailor-made gown." DR. JALAP : "Yes, lam going to retire. I've got enough and am willing to give somebody else a :thence." Fogg: "I see. Your motto henceforth will be 'Live and let live.'" Mits. Frank Stuart Park, an American dress reformer, nays that the staylace has "filled more graves than whisky." Of corset has. WHAT is the difference between a boy and a very pretty bonnet ?....One becomes a man and the other becomes a woman. "IT is really very odd, my dear," said an old lady one very hot day to a friend; "I can't bear the heat in summer, and in winter I love it." "I WISH I was twins," said Willie. "Why?" "I'd send the other half of me to school, and this half would go fishing." Haitnx : " Si she refused you, did she ?" Jack: "Yes, and I shall remember what she said as long as I live." Harry : " What did she say?' Jack: "She said 'No.'"

"MY dear," said a father, "you must marry a man of mature age; what think you of a husband of fifty?" "I think two of twenty five would be better, papa." MAGISTRATE (to prisoner); "Have you any remarks to make ?" Prisoner (a barber): "Yes, your worship. Your hair wants cutting." Su& —"Since my return from the south of France I'm another woman." Sarcastic Friend— "flow delighted your husband must bet" 138—'riAattie, If I only dared to kiss you I" She—" Harry, whatever you are, don't be a -coward." You can flatter any man by telling him that you know him to be a man who is not easily ' flattered. JUDGE : "If I let you off this time will you promise not to come back here again 7" Prisoner : "Yes, sir. The fact is, I didn't come voluntarily tbis time." THE limnEit EDUCATION.--" It has cost you a good deal to put your son through Oxford ?' "Yea.' "Do you think It is likely to pay you ?" " Well, I expect so. He has already received one offer from a profenional rowing club." RECTOTiS WIFE (severely): "Tommy Jackson, how is it that you don't take off your hat when you meet me?" Tommy :" Well, mama, if I take oft my hat to you what be I to do when I meet the parson hinise'l?" OBEDIENT BOYS. —Mother : "When I gave each of you boys an orange, Johnnie, you said you would not eat yours until after dinner, and you Archie, said the same. Have you deceived me?" Johnnie: "No, ma, we didu t eat our own oranges. I ate Archie's and he ate mine." SAID a pompous husband, whose wife had stolen up behind and given him a kiss—" Madam, I consider such an act indecorous." "Excuse me," said the wife, "I didn't know it was you." "PAPA, Augustus has made me an offer of msrriage." " What-- you don't tell me you wish to marry that fellow! First he sett up as an artist, then he invented a balloon, then he was shut up in a lunatic asylnm, and now he makes you an offer of m.rriage • Votes (at the telephone): "Major, will you plese bring your family and take supper with U 8 next Sunday 1" Servant Girl (replies back through telephone) : "Master and mistress are not in at present, but they can't come to supper, as it's my Sunday mite SuseictoNs AROUSED.—Mother: "What a nice big wheelbarrow your p ipa has bought you." Bobby (g,oomily) :"I wish he'd got me a littler one." Mother : " Why ?" Bobby: "I'm 'fraid he'll want ins to help him in the garden now with this."

A CASE OF NECESSITY.—BIoomer : "I under- stand that you have bought a cottage at the sea- side for this summer." •De Tootville :"I bought two, aide by side.' Bloomer " What do you want two for, with your small family ?" De Toot- ville "One is for my wife's lugvage." MILS. COBWIOCFER, : "I don't see how you can move so otten. It must play havoc with your furniture." Sirs. Parvenu "Of course it does, my dear; but just think how it adds to my colleo- tion of bric-a-brac !" "Mildred, will you be my wife? " She: " Well, not to-day." He : "Oh, Mildred, how can you speak so flippantly ? " She: " Flippantly ? How do you suppose I could possibly be your wife today? I should want at least two weeks to get ready in." ROOMER who has just seen the landlady's daughter for the first floe): "That's a lovely creature downstairs." His chum (who has heard her sing): "Soreecher, did you say ?" "SHE is very handsome, and they say she is very pious." " Yes, she belongs to the Society of Christian Endeavour." "Do you think you've made any impression on her?" " She is trying to convert me." "By Jove you're in luck I She not only wants you for this world, but for the next." " Mns. SMALL," said the lodger to his landlady, "I thought you didn't allow smoking in the sitting. room?" "I don't,' replied Mrs. Small with energy. "Who's doing it, I'd like to know ? In many particulars the difficulties of dress are becoming simplified. A charming evening gown for a young girl was made in light yellow satin Surah, tke skirt tucked in broad stripes, divided by lace insertion of the new butter colour, a decided yetlow, with no dash of twine or 6.3tir in it. These tuckinge were not continued quite to the edge, which was allowed to fall free and so form a &neer). The bodice fastened behind, underneath a perpendicular band of insertion, which com- ple,ely hid the opening. There were several rows of lace at the back, the front being slightly full and ending round the barque in a frill of laoe, making a most becoming bodice. The new Parisian milinery include one or two models allowing the new colours—a briliiant cerise, or a fuchsia red. A bonnet of the cerise was made of the new moire velvet, with upstanding bows and a puff a the material on each side, giving the necessary breadth to the bonnet iadispsusable to all fashionable headgear. It was lined with black, and had two rosettes on each side at the back. A Mario Stuart bonnet showed another novelty, ns.reely, a' brim edged with kid, embroidered in black beads; while another bonnet was composed entirely of pink, lined with black velvet, turned up with two points in front, and trimmed with an aigrettee. It was made out of a square of the kid worked in jet on that portion which forme the ciown. •

Amongst Parisian hats, was ablaok beaver tonne, lined with white kid, ands o turned up at the side that the white lining showed. It Was trimmed with jet laid on to.the white kid, and it was orna- inented with black tips at the side. The Napoleon shape in hats is a popular one, and a felt hat of this kind had a crescent on one side and tips and rosattes on the other, while a blank picture hat in beaver was lined with velvet and trimmed with plumes. A delightful bonnet is made of a drab, saft felt, turned up to form two erect ends in the front, which is decked with sable tails and a knot of torquoise-blue velvet resting on the hair, while the back shows another bow of the torquise blue. Some tea jackets I saw lately were moat pretty. Oue was of scarlet surah, made with the fashion- able double basque. The collar at the back. was in box pleats and turned down; in front it was plain and turned back with large points, leaving a slightly open neck in the shape of a V. A broad fichu of lace fell from under the collar, over the sleeves, and reached to the waist back and front. The double basque was edged with narrow guipure, and so were the collar and the large turned-back cuffs on the sleevLs; these, h;ch were full, reached a little below the elbow, and from them there hung broad lace like that forming the fichu. Another tea jacket the effect of which was light and airy, was of heliotrope silk, the fichu arrangement being made of rows of silk Indian muslin, and narrow Valenciennes insertion.

A tambourine can be made into a lovely work. basket by ',covering the bottom with quilted satin in any co:our and lining the sides with velvet of a controving colour. A cover is made by covering round piece of cardboard with velvet, and attach- ing it to the tambourine with straps of ribbon. A gathered section of satin is arranged on the inside of the cover, and below the satin is placed a rounded piece of velvet, having ribbon sown down at, intervals, and through these loops are arranged the artie.as needed for fine sewing.

bfantles this season are quite uncommon. A cape, for example, of striped brown zibeline, or rather a triple cape, each bound with a fold of green velvet reaching below the knee, had a gathered frill of the same round the shoulders, closely pleated on the top of the arm and inter mixed with brown and gold passernenterie. A green ostrich feather ruff at the neck was tipped with brown and black. It was especially suitable for wearing over large sleeves. A close fitting jicket of heliotrope cloth was short at-the back and long in the front ; large bows of black velvet, edged with jet fringe, being introduced on the shoulders, while down the centre of the back and on the long fronts a medimval design of painted velvet was introduced, the pattern outlined with beads. The sleeves were large and closely pleated, and the collar stood out in points round the face. A very elegant fur-lined three-quarter cape was edged with fur, with pointed shoulder capes.

A very charming costume ia male of a brown fancy cloth in a soft shade, combined with petunia velvet. It takes the form of a long coat, with velvet sides, cut :-quare from the fitting over a cloth vest which fastens invisibly. 'l ha sleeves have a full puff of the cloth at the top, falliis; over a tight-fitting velvet sleeve, the velvet being out- lined with flee sequin gimp. The skirt, which is of apshort walking,length, has three thick rolls of velvet round the foot. A seasonable walking costume consists of a semi. loose coat, three-quarter h ngth, in tan cloth, adorned with cord, !cogs, ecrolis, and large ELI-1p buttons, together with mmlitash fur, bands of which are carried round the throat and fall loose in two boa ends partly held down by the military fastening: Biscuit-coloured gown full all round, and encircled with rows of ribbon in e'lestunt- brown velvet. Brown felt hat, trimmed with back velvet ribbon and cluster of cocks' feathers, sets off the whole very nicely. Yours affectionately, J ENNIE.

OR " &Or-MYSTERY OF BUCK-TOR LIGHTHOUSE,
BY Leone JAW 'ABBEY, Author of !‘,lone, the Pride of . the Mill," N., &a. CHAPTER XIII. 8.! I WOULD RATHER NEE YOU DEAD, IN YOUR YOUTH 4 AND FAIR BEAUTY, THAN HIS BRIDE."

We must now return to the thrilling scene transpiring in the underground apartment in which beautiful Verlie Sefton found herself, by the force of strange circumstances, an unwilling prisouer. When Verlie awoke to consciousness the great pansy-blue eyes flared open wide, wandering around the strange apartment in which she found herself; then up into the hoe bending over her in the ut- most bewildeiment.

"Where am 1? she gasped, faintly. "And who are you? " Black Hagar showed her ivories in a broad grin. "Iq3 your nurse, chile," she answered, " an' the pusson who jes left am yer doctor." "Have I been ill ? " whispered Verlie, incredu• lously. " Yer ankle war sprAned, honey, an' the doctor war fetched to ket " Oh, I remember! I remember!" shrieked Pettit) in terror. "The duel—and—all that happened after it If , this is your house I pray you to let me go at once," she soubed, clinging to the old woman's skirts in a transport of grief pitiful to behold. "Those who love me are searching for we in anguish that is more bitter to bear than death. I have a darling sister whose heart must have broken when she returned to the spot whece she left me lying unconscious and found me—gone! I dare not picture it I Oh, Uldene 1 Uldene I

"And there is another 1" she sobbed piteously— "another who loves me, and who had only that evening asked me to be his bride Oh I what must he be suffering, my handsome, noble love, whom I love so dearly, as the horrible hours drag their slow lengths by,! How he must have searched for me I He will go through fire and flood, search the whole world through, but what he will find me ; and those who have detained me hero will feel the full force of his vengeance. "Oh, Rutledge? my love 1 my love 1" moaned Verlie. "Heaven grant that you may find me soon 1" "It's many a long day afore yer lover would think o' findin, yer ha'ar, honey," laughed Black Hagar. 'Oh, if I could but persuade you to help me to get away from here I " sobbed Verlie. "He who mourns my loss so keenly would reward you with plenty of gold if you would but help me." "Chile, I wouldn't dare ter do it," declared Bleak Hagar. "Ise powerful 'fraid of the cap'n. He am a reg'lar debbal. He brung yer ha'ar him- self, an' says he, when he left de room, 'Hager, iso gwine ter leave dat gal under yer eye, an' of I don't find she am ha'ar when I cum back, I wouldn't give much for yet. ole black hide; you min' my words 1' So you see, honey, I wouldn't dare ter. Why, chile, he'd murder me 1 He am none ter good ter do it." "Oh, Heaven I what awful fate has conspired spinet me ?" sobbed Verlie, wringing her little hands. "I cannot see where all this will lead to. Oh, pity me, Hagar 1 If you will not set me free, kill me I Better death than that I should fall into the hands of the man who brought me here." " Lor', chile, don't yer talk like that. Old Hagar wouldn't tech one ha'ar o' yer golden head for all Macao Cap'n's ill-gotten gold. Guess not But let me give yer a bit o' adwice, honey. For de good Lor's sake, chile, don't go for to rilin' of him up. Yer don't know de cap'n like I do. 'Member ole Hagar's warnin'. De cap'n am a fierce debbil."

Left to herself, Verlie thought over the situation until she grew frantic with terror. "Had Heaven shut her out from its mercy ?" she asked herself. There we.s no sleep for Verlie as the hours dragged by. It was well for her that there was not. As she lay there thinking over some plan by which she might make her escape, the sound of cautious foot- steps fell upon her ear ; they drew nearer and nearer, and the blood froze in Verliei veins, as they halted outside the door. She gave a suppressed cry. "Hush 1 ' whispered a voice which she instantly recognised as the captain's. "As you value your safety—hush 1 lam here on an errand which con- cerns you vitally. You must listen to what I have to say. Send Hagar to unbar the door; every moment is precious." "Iwlll not unbar the door," cried Verlie. "I am thankful that those bolts form even a slight protection in keeping you out." "You mult listen to what I have to say to you," repeated the young captain, sternly ; "it is a matter of life and death, I assure you upon my honour."

"A life, or a death, for that matter, weighs little with you," retorted the girl, bravely; " and as for honour —a man who wilfully abducts a young girl, and keeps her a captive, because she has by chance stumbled upon the nefarious calling of himself and his wicked associates, is dead to the word honour. I would not trust you." "I know full well that I have forfeited your respect by what you have seen and heard, be said, in an agitated whisper, " but there is this much honour about me—l must warn you of the fatal consequences your discovery, and your per- sistent assertions that you would bring the officers of the law upon us the first moment we set you free has brought upon you. "The men's solemn conference has ended. They intend to show you no mercy. The sentence they have passed upon you is imprisonment for life within these walls, and that would be worse than death for you. Aye, death would be a thousand timee, more merciful than life among these lawless men. Even if you did consent to au oath of silence now, it would be too late." Verlie did not faint; she did not cry out, or utter any moan ; the horror of his words held her spell-bound. She was young and brave—life Deemed sweet to her. She realised that what he said was perfectly true. These outlaws, who could thus defy the laws of men, would have no scruple in defying the law of God ; even if they made away with her, the world would be none the wiser. _

"There is but one escape for you," whispered her captor, "and that is, to become my bride. I am a reckless, defiant man, Miss Sefton ; but your beauty won my heart at first sight. The abhorrence in your beautiful eyes awoke me to a sense of my downfall from the ranks of honour. able men. Be my wife, and you shall leave this place for ever. A wife could give no evidence against her husband ; you would—" "Stop I" cried Val he ; "I will not listen." "I beg you s ill take time to consider," he said, earnestly. "I need no time to consider," replied Verlie, with ringing sewn. "Do you think that freedom or life itself is worth purchasing at the cost of becomlni your wife ?" cried, the girl, with pas. Monate vehemence. "Do you think I could clasp the hand at the altar that was stained with blood 7" The man upon the other side of the cavern door wineed under the scathing words. In-her long conversations with the leading members of Mr. Hare's company at 'Balmoral recently the Empress Eugene pathetically reminded them that 23 years had passed since she last witnessed a play. Paolo Mantegazza, of Florence, has been recently giv- ing his opinion in. a German paper on the women of Europe. To the Spanish woman he gives the palm for beauty. " The Spanish woman," he rays, "is bewitch- ingly beautiful. She has small hands and feet, and large eyes like the open windows of a sunburnt marble palace. A figure full of grace and life, and long wavy dark hair. he is very religious, very ignorant, very jealous, sensitive, idle, and proud." ' Miss Ray Frank of Oakland, Cal, is to be ordained soon asa rabbi of the Jewish %lurch, and wll be the first of her sex, it is said, to occupy such a position. She has been gullying at the Californian State University and at the Hebrew Union College-at Cincinnati. In her interesting volume of recollections just pub- lished, Miss Louisa Twining tells of how one of the in- mates, in connection with her home for workhouse girls, received from the Strand Union, bore the name of Vic- toria Queen, being a foundling picked up on the Queen's birthday. On leaving the home she obtained a situa- tion at Twickenham, and while there became engaged to a carpenter with the appropriate name of Albert Edward to whom she was happily married. Old age is honourable in. China, and the consequence is that the women of the Flowery Kingdom know how to grow old gracefully.; at least they do it without out- ward and visible protest. When the summers and win- ters of four or five decades have whitened her hair and contracted her features, the Chinese woman makes no effort to conceal the ravages of time. She ceases to mako her toilet of any account;. her garments are ex- tremely plain, her hair smoothed back without orna- ment or flower, jewel or pin to hide its faded lustre. This is universal, no matter what rank of the woman.

- Dyeing a Coat. • Procure from any chemist a bottle of Judson's dye for sixpence. Put the coat into an earthen basin of boiling water (from two to four quarts) for a few minutes Lift the coat out with a clean stick, and into tne same water pour a little of the dye.. The quantity depends upon the shade required. Too little is better than too much, as more can be added if needed. Put the coat into the water again, and stir it quickly about with a stick in each hand from five to fifteen minutes. When the article is of sufficiently deep shade, remove it from the water, and hang it out to dry. Until quite dry the colour will not show. 4

Christmas Cake. 'This is an excellent recipe for a Christmas cake, and should be made now :—lngredient—One pound flour, 1 lb. sugar, 2 114. currants, lb. almonds, 1 lb. butter, *lb. lemon peel, 9 eggs, one tablespconful of brandy. Melt the butter and sugar together' then add the flour, currants (well washed and dried), lemon peel (chopped fine), and almonds .(blanched end cut rather small). When all these are well mixed together, add the eggs, which should be beaten separately. Stir well, put into tins lin‘d with greased Faper, and bake in a hot oven at first and then moderate the heat. No time should be stated for the taking .of such cakes, as much depends up- on the oven, but try with a knitting needle wken they have been baking about two hours. If the mixture is put into a number of small tins, the cakes will take less time to bake.

, Insects and Human Beings. Grubs, worms, weevils, beetles. Eco., found in food are not, says Dr. Allinson, harmful as a rule to human beings. Fat white grubs in peas, tnans, pears, plums, nuts, raspberries, ice., are killed by gastric juice and nourish a little. The same of maggots in mushrooms. The grubs in figs and dates, too, • are harmless, if acci- dentally taken. Even maggots found on fly blown meat are not injurimls. The small green flies found on let- tuces may be swallowed by the dozen if &sir( d. Worm, in flour, and grubs or beetles in monkey nuts, are not injurious to eat. Irtrge greon catnpillars may be eaten with impunity. All grubs living on fruit or vegetables, as a rule, are harmless if purposely swallowed, being in this respect like maggots in cheese. Vegetarians, of course, do not eat caterpillars. Harmful parasites exist. Wash vegetables in salt and water.

There is a Jiability of disease germs in the dust, and dirt adheres to the ordinary wear of any person during the day, and it is wise therefore always 0 brush your clothing every tinte you change it after a day's use of it.

"Better a dry morsel," says the wise man of Israel, " and quietness therewith than a house full of sacrifices with strife." The persistent argumentator is a most disagreeable dinner companion. At meals at least people have a right to expect pleasant talk, and even the merest trivialities are more welcome than the sug- gestion of strife or argument.

div.head: BANKRUPTCY OF MAJOR JAMES
div.p: THE BANKRUPTCY OF MAJOR JAMES
CROSS, OF WIDNES.

At the Wrexham Bankruptcy Court, on Tuesday , Major James Cross, QR., at present residing at' , Llangollen. but formally carrying on business at Widnes, again came up for his public examination. ' The statement of affairs showed gross liabilitis amounting to .£85,105 17.1. 6d.; the assets were put down at 77 bs. 71., and there was an estimated , deficiency of £10,591 10. From 1865 to the Bth of August. last the debtor was managing trustee .to the Hutchinson estate, Widnes, and from 1864 to 1868 he traded as a locomotive builder at Helens, under the style of James Cross and Co. In the latter year he became insolvent, the smaller creditors being paid in full, and the larger oneis receiving 10+. in the pound. He again failed in the present year, his insolvency being due as he alleged, to his becoming surety for a Mr. J. W. Weight, a London stor, kbroker, for £8,909 Ile claimed. however, that if he had receivid all that Ile was entitled to from the Hutchinson estate, he was solvent. The examinatioo was adjourned from the previous court to enable the bankrupt to supply to the court a statement of the vari- oos financial transactions in which he had hcsai engaged with various people.—The Oftic4d Receiver (Mr. LI. Hugh Junes), asked the debtor why he had no include. in Els statement of accotiuts 157 C shares in the Widnei and Ditton Land Company.—Major Cross said they were of no value, and there was a heavy liability on them They had not been cancelled or forfeited. Chere were £lO shares, and £2 had been paid on them. A resoltit had been passed by the company to call up the £8 due on the shares, but no call had het n paid. Ho d not think any purchaser could be found for the 175 shares at pre:ent.—The Official Receiver : Apart from these shares, is there anything, whether valuable or not,that you have not disclosed ?—Major Cross : Ni. —The examination was closed.

paesea instantaneously before hie mental vision. He could imagine a lost soul gazing from the deep abyss of Hades into the felicity and joy of Heaven, fully realising that all hope for him was lost for ever. He began to realise that a dark chasm yawned between himself and this fair girl; a fatal line streaked his hand, which would forever shadow the grasp of a purer one. It Is a mistake to suppose that crime-steeped souls cannot love. The basest criminal, strange as it may seem, can love as intensely, though not as purely or unselfishly, as the noblest hero. From the moment his eyes had rested upon the beautiful girl who had dared defy him 80 bravely and audaciously, the wiah came to this bad man that he had lived a different life that he might have wooed and, in time, won her. A moment he hesitated. "Do you love any one else I Will yAmi answer me that, Miss Sefton V" "Yes," came the quivering reply, in a choked, girlish voice, "I do. If you had not detained me here I should now be the betrothed bride of a good and noble man, one who could never stoop to a dishonourable action and whom I love with all my heart. Oh, sir, would it be of any use to plead with you to restore us to each other? Mr. Rut- ledge Chester would reward you well for aiding me, I am sure." The man started back as though an arrow had suddenly piereed.hia heart. • "What I" he cried fiercely, "is Rutledge Chester the man you love—that man, above all other men, whom I have reason to hate so bitterly —the man that made me what I am, drove me from the ranks of honourable men by exposing me, and made me a hunted criminal on the face of the earth? Restore you to him? I would see you dead W my feet first 1 Why, his very name rouses a very demon in my heart! And to think that he should have crossed my path again—that he, of all others, should have won the love of the only being I have ever met whom I could care for. It is mad- dening 1 "1 vowed once that I would pay him back, at a bitter cost, for what happened in the past. I Bee Ai way now to that very end. I bided my time. No, you shall never go free, save as my wife I " We are preparing to leave this place in the course of a mouth for a lengthy voyage, but you go with us. Remember, I would rather see you dead at my feet—in all your youth and fair young beauty—than see you Rutledge Chester's bride 1" He stood away from the door, his handsome face fairly livid with satanic rage; but his last words had fallen upon deaf ears. Verlie had fainted. " Was there ever such a tangled web woven by inexorable fate?" he muttered, twisting the ends of his moustache. "She loves Rutledge Chester."

div.head: YOUNG GULL.
div.p: YOUNG GULL.

In the intense darkness of the cavern he did not see the slim, girlish figure that had followed him close to the door, and had listened, with bated breath and face pale as death, to every word that had been uttered.

"He cares for this beautiful stringer," • she muttered, with a dry, hard sob. "Oh, what a rude awakening from my dreatn. I thought he loved me. His eyes said so even though his lips did not. I might one day have been his bride if this golden-haired girl had not come between us with her pretty face. Oh, fatal day for me that she was brought here I" Going around by another entrance, and passing through Hagar's apartment, she found herself in Verlie's presence.
With s-wift-s—t-e-is she crossed the room and stood, with darkening brow, gazing down upon the prostrate figure the swinging lamp dimly revealed to her.

Ah, the stranger was more beautiful than any poet's dream, with her white' delicately-chiselled face, framed in its sheen of floating golden hair, upturned to the dim light. A bitter pang of jealousy smote the girl's heart as she gazed. As if attracted by that magnetic gaze, Verlie's white eyelids fluttered open, and she looked up in dismay into the face bending over her. Ile next moment she has struggled to her knees, clinging to the girl's skirts with an sgony of entreaty pitiful to " Will you help me to leave this place?" she pleaded, frantically. "You are a young girl like myself. You must be tender of heart. I Implore you to aid me. Restore ma to my friends, and you shall be well rewarded for it. Think how they must suffer. It will break my poor father's and mother's hearts wken they are told of my strange disappearance." "You would not like to accept the alternative that would release you from this place? You would rebel against wedding the man who brought you here?" the girl asked, breathlessly, a strange glitter in her eyes as she spoke. "The very thought would drive me to madness," moaned Verlie, with passionate vehemence.

"I will help you to leave this very night upon one condition," answered the girl shortly. "And that ?" whispered Vedic:breathlessly. "And that," repeated the girl, in a hurried whisper, "is that you take an oath of silence never to reveal this retreat, and never to mention to a living being what you have seen or heard from the fatal hour you chanced to witness that duel to this. I have a father and a brother here, and one whom I love better than life. For their sake I must exact a solemn vow of secrecy, or I dare not aid you. Don't you see?' " Yes," said Verlie, huskily. "I can under- stand the situation, and for your sake I would vow eternal secrecy.' 'You could say, without going far from the truth, that you were found with a sprained ankle, and taken care of until you were able to be about, . and that, being delirious, your friends could not be communicated with. Yon must make haste if you would escape to-night," the girl went on, with a strange thrill of excite- ment in her voice, " for it is almost daylight now.

She silenced the joyful cry on Verlie's lips by saying, huskily : " You must wear my cloak and my broad hat. You -;,an discard them, and leave them at the first bend in the road, beneath the tall oak there, and don your own. There is but one exit, and that leads through a room in which a number of the men are congregated. You must trust to your own bravery to pass you through that trying ordeal; it will be fraught with greatest danger. If any one should call out to you or speak to you, make some excuse. Your voice is not unlike mine."

She threw her own dark waterproof cloak over Verlie, who noticed, as those slim hands touched her, how they trembled, and how death-cold they were. At last Verlie, quivering with suppressed excite- ment, stood ready. She had given her solemn promise to that which her rescuer required.

ft You Will give me your name," she whispered, " that I may never cease to bless you for what you have done for me this night." "You must know me only as Kelpie; that is what they call me here. When you are home with your friends, when you are happy with him whom you love, you will sometimes think of me, will you not?" she asked. "And whenever you think of Kelpie, forget her surroundings. Think of hr kindly, and at her best, Go now," she added, drawing her ice cold hands from erlie's clasp. "Follow that winding cavern to the ed. That will be to freedom. Good•bye and may God speed you." She threw the door open wide, and, like a storm. driven swallow, panting with fear at every step, Verlie flew down the narrow, subterranean, wind- ing passage. She had nearly reached the end of the passage, when, turning a sharp curve, she found livrself confronted by two men. Verlie's heart seemed to contract with sudden fear. She dared not turn buck, and a few feet more would bring her abreast of them. If they discovered her identity, all was lost. She nerved herself for the terrible ordeal. One of the men turned his head and saw her. "Why, Kelpie," he said, approaching her, "what in the world takes you out before daybreak? IVhat arc you up to now? Some mischief, I'll be bound." "Only a walk," replied Peril°, her heart palpitating so pitifully loud she was quite sure he must hear its beating, in her great anxiety and terror lest she failed to make her voice sound just like Kerpie's. "Would you mind having company I" he asked, banteringly. She shook off his hand from her arm, and dashed past him before he could obtain a good view of her face. A moment more, and—oh, joy I joy I—she had emerged into the grey, dull, misty morning light; the free air of heaven blew across her face. "How strangely Kelpie acts," saki the man, 4.71,22,00.tex the ;tying, slim, girlish figure,

" She bas not been the same space the lovely, golden-haired little beauty was brought here," laughed his companion. She's afraid the cap- tain has fallen in love with her: and that's just exactly what he's done. It's a pity, for poor Kelpie is so fond of him." Both laughed and hurried on. Meanwhile, Verlie found herself once more in the old isolated cemetery, where the fatal accident had happened which had led to such grave results. Ihe swollen, sprained ankle, which had not had time to mend properly, commenced paining again acutely, and by the time she had reached the' main road, became so excrutiating that poor Verlie threw up her hands and fell, face downward, in the snow-drifts in a dead faint, with the name of Rutledge on her quivering lips. NVhen the sun rose, pink and golden, over the eastern hills, it fell upon her upturned face, hrlf veiled by the sweeping golden hair that trailed over the white drifts. Her hands were locked closely together, low moans issuing from her lips. A young man, (hiving hurriedly along, suddenly drew rein by the roadside, and gazcd, with a cry of surprise on his lips. "A young and beautiful girl 1" he ejaculated, in great astonishment, as Is leaped from the sleigh. " What can she be doing here, I wonder ?" He touched the lovely little white hands gently. They were burning hot. Carefully he raised the slight figure, and placed it in his sleigh. "It is clearly evident that I cannot leave her here," he mused. It seemed such a pity to take that fair young creature to a charity hospital. Then a sudden idea occurred to him. Why not take her home? His mother, of all people in the world, would know just what to do for the beauti- ful, hapless young stranger. It was scarcely ten miles to his home, if he took the by-ways. To teach it in a roundabout way by the road was over twice the distance. Turning his horse's head, he gave the spirited animal a cut with his whip, and away they went spinning over the white, crusted snow. Within an hour he had drawn rein before a fine country house, sprung from the sleigh, and was hurrying up the broad gravel walk toward the door. A young girl, brown as a gipsy, who had been out on the side porclkfeeding the snow-birds, gave a slight scream. "On, mother, mother 1 do come here, quick, and see what brother Dick has in his arms 1 It looks like a coffin—no—Ws a young girl!" she exclaimed in breathless dismay. By this time Mr. Richard Temple had reached the carious young romp, who had bounded down the path to meet him, fairly bristling with curiosity.

" For mercy's sake, whom have you got there, Dick V she cried, with great, wild, dilated eyes. "Who in the world is that, and what's the matter with her ?" "Don't ask so many questions, Edna l" ex- claimed her brother, impatiently. " Run on to the house and open the door, and get mother ; and run quick and see if there's hot water, and blankets, and mustard and peppermint. Now, for goodness sake, don't stand there staring, Edna, with your eyes and mouth wide open. Don't you see this poor thing is nearly dead? I don't know what's the matter with her."

"Great goodness I" ejaculated Edna, with a low whistle. "You don't say so l' The gypsyish tom- boy always exasperated Mr. Temple. "Edna," he cried, impatiently and sharply, "will you run ahead to open the door or not V' "Of course," gasped Edna' atill staring with all her might at the slim figure he held in his arms. But, alas I for Edna's headlong haste—she never could be depended on in cases of emergency—with every step forward she slipped back two, and as Richard Temple crossed the porch he looked back just in time to see the black, curly head and a pair of heels scrambling out of a huge snow- drift, into which she had been precipitated head- long. . _

div.head: WERE THESE DOCTORS IGNORANT.
div.p: WERE THESE DOCTORS IGNORANT.

" jot it int') my head that the doctors didn't under- stand nq eontpitthit." Whence did she get that notion? Can it be possible that the doctors are often at a loss what to do for us ? and that too, at times when our very, fives are in their hands ? There is no denying that our confidence in th-in gets awfully shaken occasionally. They Come at our call, they feel our pulse, they use big words, they look very deep and clever—but alas! it often ends in that they can't do anything. And, after all they send in their bills! To be sure, for doctors must live some- how. But we don't mind if they could only cure. That's what they are educated for, and paid for. Well, well ; what made Mrs. Harriet lladden susrect rhe medical man ? Possibly she isn't giving them fair play. Her stNry is short and straight, and after we have read it we shall be better able to judge. Here is her letter, dated March 31st, 1892, and sent from her own home, 4, Foundry-at, Raiff ird, N ttingham. "I have," she sap', " sutTered from biliousness nearly 311 my life. Ali, u; six years ago I began to be seriously ill. I felt tired, weak, and languid, and was constantly vomiting a greenish, bitter fluid. My skin was sallow. ' and the whites of my eyes a yellow colour. My appe- tite was poor, and after eating I had great pain at the chest and sides. There was a sinking feeling at the pit of the rtomach and my inside was all of a flutter. Gra- dually I got weaker and weaker until I could scarcel drag m sAf along. I grew so nervous that I -hook all ,ver and could hardly lift a cup to my lips. Often the pain in my stomach was 'so intense that I thought a tumour or cancer must be growing there. Later on I btcame very stiff in the joint and was troubled with cramp and rheumatism in the legs and arms.

'• I consulted doctor after doctor (I saw five or six in all), trim gave me medicines; but I got worse. .1 was so bad that for weeks together I hallo keep b my bed. " In April, 1888, I got a recommendation Cram Mr. Manlove to the Nottingham Infirmary, where I was treated for eight weeks, but without relief. I got it intro my head that the doctors did not understand my com- plaint, and that I should never get better. In this was' I went on suffering until one day in November, 1890, my little grand-daughie • came to my bedside arid said, Grandmother, I have brought you a book.'

" I read in the book about, a peram who hid suffered jut as I had and been cured by Mother Seigel's Cutative Syrup. I sent for the medicine and began taking it,and in t days twas down stairs, feeling better than I had done for years. Leaving off all other medicine, I kept on with the Syrup, anti soon all the pain left tne, I digested my food and got rtionger every day. By tak- ing an occasional dose, I continued in good health. If I had only used it years before, when a friend of mine, Miss ToU le, of Trafalgar-street, advised me to, I should have been saved great suffering and heaw/ dodoes' bills." (Signed) Yours truly, lialittlET HADDEN. Now, in view of all this shall we agree with Mrs. Had- den that the dont ws didn't erbderstand her complaint? [bey had treated her for at least six years, and left her worfe than. vrlieNthey coroinenceal. What does that mean? Would they not have cured her if they could? Certainty. Then wby ilidn't they? There is but one answer: they did not because they could not. Before her case all their study and learning went for nothing, and It as than notl In, hr while they dallied and doubted precious time ran to waste and the patient tot- !ti red towards the grave. Yet these doctors were pro- tiably as god as most of them. And.this is not a rare example; otheis like it can be heard of all ov. r the coun- try. t'o important and dreadful is the conclusion, that we will not now put it in plainer woidti. People can see (or t hems, .V 6-1.

Tie reti I unr:an entAl disease in this inetance was in- digestion and dysier sia, of si hith all the good woman's P°s and pains were 83mi tome. The doctors may not understand this, but lother ,'.4c.igel did, and her medicine cures it. The sooncr everybody is aware of this, the POMO' will the suffi ring one get ell ; and the more and pounds will they rave to pay for lie't Pitiatirta•

div.head: PRETENSION.
div.p: PRETENSION.

-- In the long run a man almost always passes in the orld for what he is personally and morally worth. very idle is all curiosity as to what other people may think of us, and all fear that we may remain unknown. What we can do and are doing is seen and virtually ac- knowledged by those who know us, and with whom we are from day to day associated. The world is full of pdgment days ; and in all the relations and actions of ife, men are gauged and stamped, and their true value Understood. All men and all things must stand on their respective Merit. Among the scientific agents which have stood the test is Warner's Safe Cure. Mrs. M. Gammon, 9, Marlow-strert, Waterloo, 13lyth, writes :—" For eight Years I suffered tom gravel and kidney disease. I :Was so bad that I could not attend to my usual housenold duties. The doetor who attended me wanted to Operate on me, but I firmly refused. I was advised to try Warner's Safe Cure. I did so, and after taking the .!Poond bottle I got relief. I persevered, and in a short utne felt so well that I was quite able to attend to my usual duties. , .1 honestly advise everyone suffering with gravel or t.tidney disease to use this remedy, and also let the world KnoW how valuable it is.

,_. .nerkeley-sq The Duke— -23, T, of Sutherland's well-known house, No. uare, is announced for sale at the freely end of this week. Berkeley-square has been patronised by many noble statesmen who I;al'e left their mark in history. Earl Granville ':_ved at No. HI, a mansion previously occupied by Chancellor Cottenham. Lord Brougham lived 21, Horace Walpole at. No. 11, and it was at • g,?. 45, on the west side of the Square, that Lord ivus death, was e died by his own hand. Clive, on the day of playing whist with Lady Clive, coearY Strachey, and Henry Strachey's wife—a cillBin of Lady Clive. At a pause in the game Lord t; `ve left the morn, and not returning for some 21e, a search was made, with the result that he "as found dead, his throat cut with a pen-knife.

War- rington had been libelled in his hearing, and he was scarcely prepared at that meeting to see so intellectual A gathering, so alive to the social problems of the day, and 90 enthusiastic an audience. He thanked them most heartily for permitting him to be present at such a gathering, and to witness such intense civic patriotism and civic pride of which Warrington was capable. Speaking as a Christian minister he saw in the movement represented that night, a new incarnation of the chris- tian spirit. Religion had as much to do with the elec- tion of the town council as with the election of deacons. They ought to pray for their rulers. He did not suppose that it would do them any harm. (Laughter.) It was • reflection upon their manhood, and upon their courage, and upon their conception of patriotism. They were now living in a new age. With all this pressure it was dangerous to take strong drink, which would have a terrible effect upon the human frame. When all this was talc;m into consideration, temperance reform was the very best of all social reform, and was the very incarnation of the spirit of Jesus Christ. (Applause.) Only one half of the country had been drinking, but the ether half was beginning now. Man had been drinking up 1000 w, but" God help us!" woman was now begin- ning. English women drank, as neither Irish, Welsh, Scotch, or even the frivolous French women ever did. This was a terrible fact, but he believed that the chris- tian church was going to kill the liquor traffic. They were going to have the direct veto which would give the people the power to say whether they wanted public- houses or not. (Applause.) His friend Mr. !tepee had been going about the country for the past 25 years with a sovereign which he would give to any magistrate who had voted for a public house next door to himself. : (Laughter.) The veto bill would simply give the people the same power as the magistrates. But why were not licensing laws put into force in Warrington. 1 here were laws existent to look after the public-house. The , public-house was a huge monopoly, and if the laws were broken by publicans, they ought to be punished relent- tasty. lie did not deny that some public-houses were conducted:in a proper manner, but that class was very scarce. A large portion got their living by encouraging drunkenness and encouraging gambling. The laws against this ought to be put into force by the Watch Committee. (Applause.) There was a large number of public-houses which had become" boozing ' dens, reek- ing with immorality, and fcetid atmoxpliere of the turf and the awful ataensphere of bestiality. A large num- ber of public-houses and he believed in Warrington had the notice in the taproom " The sporting papers taken here." He was sure that this made trie public-houses centres of gambling. Ile was of ' opinion that if the work was not properly done by the authorities, it was the business of every patriotic citizen to search out those houses themselves. Let them become vigilante and policemen themselves, and institute prowcutictis against the houses ins remorseless manner. It was the business of the Social Questions Union to engage in this work.and he hoped that they would be supported, and that they would go into this conflict in the strength of God. (Applause.) Mr. MONKS next moved the following resolution : " That this meeting of inhabitants of Warrington in view of the unsatisfactory attitude hitherto assumed by the Watch Committee is regard to the enforcement of the licensing laws, concerning drueltenness. gimbling, and immorality, strongly urges the new Watch Com- mittee to vigorously administer these laws, and it fur- ther affirms the general principle that no person directly or indirectly interested in the liquor traffic sheuid act on the Wateh Committee." Mr. E. J. GORST. J.P., seconded the resolution, and in doing so said the meetine was one of the most instruc- tive and interesting he had attended in the town. (Applause.) If the men and women who were present took to heart earnestly all that had been said, and did their best to follow it out, Warrington could easily be transformed into a soberer and healthier town. (Applause.) He believed there were publicans in tine town who did their best to keep their houses in accord- ance with the law ; but they had so many cases of drunkenness brought before them at the Court that it WAS hard to understand how the publicans escaped. There was else a vast amount of immorality in the town. It therefore behoved them to vote the right way and to elect councillors who would see that the Watch Commit- tee was a satisfactory one. (Applause.) They wanted better men on the Council. (Applause.) Ile hoped the people of Warrington would stand round good men in the future,and encourage them in their work. (Applause.) Mr. Roberts had set a noble example recently ; he des- erved encouragement, and he hoped they would not fail to grant it, and help him to work for the just adminis- tration of the law. (Applause.) The resolution was put to the tneetiog and Carried unianimously. Councillor H. Remmers who was received with loud applause, said he supposed he stood before them that night as a notorious character. (Laughter and ap- plause.) lie had dared to defy the authority of the Mayor of Warrington, and he had not apologised. (Applause.) And he WU not going to apologise. (Re- newed applause.) There were some people who believed that because they had a Town Clerk in Warrington who WAS peel to advise the Council upon local matters, Viet therefore the Council must swallow every piece of ad- vice and abide by every rule the Town Clerk chose t offer. (Applause.) Now, Providence for seine purpose had endow it him with a certain amount of brains, and as far as was possible he Intended to use those brains. (Applause.) And he did not intend ever to respect any piece of ruling that was not based upon common sense, and, AS in Lille particular case, which was distinctly illezal, as he understood It. (Applause.) There were acme people who said that it always required a lawyer to interpret an Act of Parliament. There was one gen. tleman in town who was one of the ablest men to b • found on poor law administration, and it was Mr. J. C. Sutton, but he had not yet been admitted into the sacred fraternity ad the legal society. (Applause.) Let th.m look at the absurd position in which it placed the Town Council. (Hear, hear.) They were called together for the purpose of electing to one of the highest posts In connection with the Council, a gentleman from among their ranks. Two names were placed before them and they were asked to vote without being allowed to make any suggestion or remark ; and be declined to be a party to any such farce. (Applause.) Ile had on lits side precedent, which had been establidied in the time of one of the •blest legal men they had had, and that WAS the late Town Clerk, Mr. %V. li. Brook, who ha/ allowed discussion and not ruled it as Illegal. (lieu, hear.) But in this case there had been a previous con- sultation between the powers that be and certain MEM- bers of the Corporation s.s to whether it would be possible to stop a discussion, because at the caucus meet- ing on the previous Monday he had declared his inten- tion to speak against the manner in which the selection hail been made. (Applause.) They muzzled him for the time being—(laughter)—but there were other reek to appeal to besides the 36 members of the Corporation There was no single man, except Alderman Platt, out of the 36 members, who had spoken one word on his be- half. ("Shame.") In that conflict he had been fight- ing for something which was valuable to them all, and which had been bought dearly—that was the right of free speeeh—and yet no one hail rendered him assistance except the gentleman be had mined. Ile asked them to look at the advice Riven by the Town Clerk in connection- .with the licensing of the theatres. It had been ruled that only the character of the ' applicant and the suitability of the place sheuld be taken into consideration In acs-5e where an excite lic,enee could be put into effect. (Bear. hear.) But he had got the advice of a higher legal authority than the Town Clerk and he should bring it forth when the opportunity served. (Applause.) This was one of the actions of the Watch Committee. It was no use talking about the Committee until they had altered the Town Council Itself. They could not get grapes off thistles. (Laugh- ter.) They might be thankful that the Wech Commit- tee was no worse. He fully expected that it would be. Ile wasn't quite prepared to see a proposition of the dominant patty to put upon the Watch Committee some of the newly elected councillors. Ile was very glad to find that they were moderate in their strength. The Social Questions Union had plenty of work beforathem to alter that state of things. It would take them years to do all that was necessary. fle was prepared to put politics upon one fide for that hour in Warrington at Y airs sod if the Conservative party or any section (Ise tit englit

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

_ In the !knee of Lords on Monday, the Savings flank Rill was read a second time on the motion of the Lord Chancellor, who explained that it would raise the amount which could be deposited in a savings bank in one year from £3O to £5O, the amount of stock which might be purchased annually from £lOO to £2OO, and the total amount from £3OO to £5OO. __

In the House of Commons Mr. Hemmer Gtanareisa. answering Mr. W. 11. Lawson, said the whole subject of the law's( distress was worthy of consideratinn.but the Secretary of State could not undertake to deal with It by legislation. Mr.GLansrosut supplemented a reply of Sir Charles Russell in reference to the Duke of Edinburgh by stating that the Duke would retain his place on the Navy List, although without pay, and without the capacity for active service. Mr. J. MOBLEY informed Mr. Yerburph that the pro- ceedings'against Mr. William Field, ALP., and Mr. Ilayden, M.P., were taken limier the common law, and not the Act of 1887. The Employers' Liability Bill, as amended by the Standing Committee, was further considered, and on the motion of the Arrosiegy.tissixuat a new clause, making contractors liable for personal injury caused by the negligence of a sub-contractor or his workmen, was added. Mr. TOMLINSON proposed the insertion of a new clause providing that an action for compensation under the Act should not be maintainable unless notice of the Injury was given within three months from its occur- rence. The clause was withdrawn, Mr. ASQUITH stating that he could not accept it, but would be willing to en- tertain the special notice in the case of seamen. Mr. Marrnms moved the insertion of a clause, exempting shipowners from liability for injury occurring outside the United Kingdom unless caused by defect in the ship or tackle &c. Mr. J. 11. WiLsois urged the claim of the sailer to have the same protection as was afforded to the verrkmen on shore. After considerable discusslen this, end several other amendments—one proposed by Mr. A. B. Fonwoop—as to the liability of shipowners were negatived. TUESDAY. In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, Sir U.. Kav-Surrutwotern, replying to it question put by Sir E. A. Bartlett as to the strength of the French fleet in the Mediterrani an, said that Ministerial answers to such questions were not calculated to improve the relations between this country and other countries with whom we were at peace. Sir E. A. Bartlett protested against being thus" lectured," and said that at the first oppor- tunity he would call attention to the subject. Mr. ASQUITH informed Mr. Darling that notice of the meeting held in Trafalgar Sqoare last Sunday was given on the 3rd October by Mr. Weiss on behalf of the mem- bers of " the Freedom Group," and the object of the meeting was stated to be the commemoration of the Chicago Anarchists and what was known as " Bloody Sunday " of 1887. He did not consider it consistent with the public interest to state whether there was any reason to suppose that the Anarchists new active on the Continent had any relations with those in this country.l Mr. Darling moved the adjournment of the House in order to call attention to the danger of permitting such ' meetings. Mr. ASQUITH said the people who aseembled in Trafalgar Square had not committed any offence against the law. If he thought there was serious danger to the public peace or to the good order of London or the kingdom in such proceedings he should certainly not allow them, but he regarded these vapourings of very Vallish and. ignorant people as having at any rate the advantage of acting as a safety-valve to feelings and opinions which were only dangereus so long as they were held in suppression. Mr. A. .1. BALFOUR said that to permit such meetings was to encourage the propaga- itien of opinions which endanzered the very foundations I, of the social system. Mr. Sense, speaking against the motion, said he believed the Anarchist tactics had led to the injury of the people's labour movement and of all other democratic movements. Alter some further discussion the motion for the adjournment of the Bowie was negatived. The House then proceeded to further consider the Employers' Liability Bill as amended.

WEDNESDAY. In the House of Commons on Wednesday, considera- tion of the Employers' Liability Bill was resumed. Mr. Tomlinson's proposal was altered, giving the employers liberty to make the person causing the injury the third party in the action, so that the master, on satisfying the plaintiff's claim, could get his remedy from the negli gent servant. On a division the dame was rejected by 162 to 61. Amendments were adopted reducing the fees parable for entering these actions in the County Court, and for their trial if desired by jury, the number of per- sons on the jury to be left open. Other amendments were discussed, and the House adjourned at half-past five o'clock.

In the nouse of Commons on Thursday evening Mr. &taw-Lai-gym{ informed Mr. W. Smith that the Royal Commission on Agricultural Depression had decided not I to admit the press to their sittings. They would publish the evidence at short dates. Mr. Bcrroti, replying to Mr. Labouchere, said he was afraid that the war had neceFsarily altered the position of aff4irs in Matabeleland, and the question became 0110 of future policy with regard to the bettlement of the country. The Employers' Liability Bill as amended by the Standing Committee was further considered, and the report stage was completed shortly after eight o'clock. The third reading was fixed for Thursdny next. On the order to go into Committee an the Local tiovernment (Parish Councils) Bill, Mr. T. Bowi.xs moved that it be an instruction to the Committee that they have power to 'divide the bill into two bill, and to embody all clauses relating to alterations In the ' Poor law in a separate bill. Mr. 11. Fowler mid he re- girded the proposed instruction is useless. After some discussion the instruction was negatived without • division. Mr. W. M'Laren moved that it be an instruc- tion to the Committee that they have power to Insert provisions to enfranchise for the purpose of the bill all those women, whether married or single, who would be entitled to be on the local government register of electors, or on the parliamentary register of electors if they were men. Mr. Fowler asked the House not to cumber the bill with this dblicult and vexed queslion. On a division the instructi in was carried ,by ICI to 126. The House then went Into Committee on ) the bill.

div.head: LOCAL LAW CASE.
div.p: A LOCAL LAW CASE.

-- At the Liverpool County Court, on Tuesday, be- fore his Honour Judge Shand and a Jury, the action of the London and North-Westorn Railway. Co. v. Garret Itonayne, of Rarleatown, for possession of a piece of land bi t list° in Earle-et,, Eeriest own, and for mesnos profits amounting to .Cl 6 :IL 21. was heard. Mr. l'reston, instructed by Mr. Bland, of the Solicitors' Department, appeared for the rail- way company, and Mr. Riley, of St. Helena, for Mr. ltonayne. The defendant had filed a counter-claim against the plaintiff company for £5OO for alleged damages austained by him in consequence of the inter- ference by the company with his enjoyment of the land in question, and also of another piece of land adjoining, running up to a railway siding also for having taken possession of certain materials iielonging to him ; for slandering his title to certain other materials and sheds, and also for interference with his business of a coal merchant and cooper. The company proved service of no, ice to quit, which expired In March, 1892. The de- fendant's counter-claim appeared to be hated upon 00 assumption that ft waiver of the notice had taken place by the plaintiff company, and defendant's solicitor, In • long crews-examination of Mr. Aveline, the Comparyy's district estate czent, tried to prove a waiver of the notice, but he was not able to do this to the satisfaction of the court, and ultimately judgment was given In favour of the Company on the claim and counterclaim with costs, possession of the land to be given in four- tern days. In giving their verdict the foreman of the jury remarked that they considered the Railway Com- pany had treated the defendant very leniently, In which remark the judge concurred.

div.head: CHILD'S ESCAPE FROM DEATH.
div.p: THE CHILD'S ESCAPE FROM DEATH.

[SPECIALLY REPORTED.] From the "News of the World," ',Auden, Oct. 15, 1893. What is known as the Forest Hill miracle having been brought to our notice, we determined to investi- gate the circumstances, in order to set at rest once and for all, by an authoritative statement from inquiries at first hand, all conflicting rumours. Briefly summarised the circumdtances are these. A little girl, crippled, and practically doomed to a wretched and painful life, cul- minating in an early death, is reported to have been "miraculously" cured, although declared hopeless by the best medical authority. lii such cases only one course can be satisfactory—a searching investigation at first hand, and a "News of the World" reporter, in a sufficiently sceptical frame of mind, was detailed to examine into the eircumstances. His report entirely confirms the statements made. The occurrence, on close investigation, proves to be exactly as described. The case (says our representative) is one of rickets, a well-known and horrible dioease, too com- mon, alas, to need description hire; the patient, a five- year old girl. Morrie Book,, by name, living with her parents at 38, F.wart-road, Forest Hill. Mrs. Hook, rejoicing at this happy results which Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People had brought about, was only too glad to give information to our representative, and thus give circulation to this wonderful cure. In answer to a question as to where Florrie might be seen, and screwing up our courage to visiting a sick bed, we were startled by the reply. " Oh, sir, Florrie's at school !" "At school, is she? Then she is completely re- covered "Yes ; completely. "has she suffered from them long " " She was born with the rickets, and haa suffered from them right up till last June." _ .
. _ " Of course you have had her: under the doctor'a care ? "

I "Oh yes, the whole time. titie.wae so ill she could not stand, and her general health was very mueli affected also. As she grew older the attacks increased In severity. I: took her to the dispensary here, but she never got any better. The doct treated her but to no purpose. In fact the disease seemed to be increasing In , severity. "And then," said our representative, "you tried Dr. Williams' Pink rills?" • yes!"

"And now you say she Is cured ?" lit the arrival upon the scone of the patient heiself, a bonny little girl of five, strong on her legs, and as lively as &cricket, particularly exuberant, too, at just getting out of. school, was the most forcible reply to this question. " Well, no MO would ever have thought that that little lady had ever suffered a day's illness. llow long did you treat her with the pills ?" "We gave her only one box. That has cured her. She got better after three days, in a fortnight she could cross the room,And in three weeks after beginning the pills she went to 'school. Before that she was quite help- less, and suffered great pain." At this moment Mr. Hook joined the party, he, too, beaming with smiles, and looking gratefully at his little daughter, anticipated the next query by saying, " And since she finished the one box she has had no sign of the disease at all ; in fact seems to get daily stronger and stronger. She is still a very little bow-legged, as you can see, but even that she is getting over. Now that she has no more suffering her lige are straightening as well as strengthening. "In fact," added Mrs. !look, vieing with her husband to bear testimony to the cure," she seems to be growing to be the strongest ofalhe whole family. I've got five children, sir. All the rest are strong 'and healthy, and now, thsnks to this trostment, Morrie lass well as any of them." We had intended asking a very budget of questions all carefully prepared beforehand, to prove to the hilt whether this treatment, and this alone, had effecteil a complete cure. But here, before our eyes, in the flesh, was a proof such as even our representative had not in his most sanguine moments anticipated. A little girl, who barely six months ago had been ab- solutely prostrate, growing daily worse and worse, and ' likely to die at any time from the effects of this scourge, a girl, too, who had the advantage of skilled medical aid, which had failed to arrest the progress of the
standing

disease, now al._ health and spirits, was a proof of the treatment so suc- cessful as to border on the miraculous. The effect, too, upon the household must not be under-estimated. Here I was the happiness of this father and mother wrecked by illness, apparently incurable. One could even now de- tect traces of past anxiety in the mother's face, but It was far easier to detect the signs of relief and comfort , that had at last come into this household of suffering." " And you would use Dr. Williams' Pink l'ills again. Mrs. Hvok "we put as a final answer. " Certainly ! That is, if I wanted it, which seems unlikely," looking, proudly at her daughter. I can always let others benefit by my own experiences. and recommend them to do as I did," and Mrs. Hook could hardly do otherwise, seeing that her household MO been bhesed by a cure that is not wittily unreason- I ably is described in the neighbourhood as a miracle. The . fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Work liotpe on Tuesday. Al r. J. Mclntyre presided, and tl:ere were present Rev. .1 W N. Tanner, Messrs. J. %% Or, E. Aaron, J. Lull H. E. Heywood, J. Parkinson, J. M. d$ illiame, T. Lewis, S. Wood- ward, W. '1 urner, C. W. Davenport, C. T. Whitley, E. Jackeen ;J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (deputy clerk), .1. Farrington (-limitary inspector.) A Nu ISANCIC AT Lame. Dr. Ormsby of Halton, wrote under date November 14. stating that it was now nearly a fortnight sinco the Clerk to the Authority told him that the Sanitary In- spector had been instructed to serve a notice on the owner of Dolly Brink, to compt to the necessary altera- tions within seven days. The Cies k hal also told him that in the event of nothing having been done before the next meeting of the Ituird (to-day)that any delay would Le the result of negligence on the part of the sanittry Authority. As )et there had not been anyone near the premises, and the nuisances atready complained of got worse in fact the escape of sewer gas into the house was horrible.—The Medical Officer of Health, . says " A wave of infection is passing over the district." lie (Dr. Ormsby) was not surprised at it, but under the circum- stances he thought it was the duty of the Sanitary Authority to make full and prompt use, impartially, of the powers it poswesed for mitigating, each individual nuisance which was brought under its notice. As far as his house was concerned, ii any: sickness attacked any ' member of his family, or himself, owing to the present condition it was in, and the apparent neglect of the Rural Sanitary Authority, he would hold them respon- sible for any loss and expense he might he put to, in addition to acl dm for dainages.—Dr. Ormsby had also written to the Local Government Hoard complaining of the inaction of the Authority in this matter, and the Loudon Board had written requesting the Authority to favour them with theirobservations thereon—The Clerk Bald Dr. Ormsby wag labouring under a mist!' ks lii mak- ing the statemea uith regard to himself.—Mr. Aaron said he believed the nuisance was very bad, and it was • time something as done.—The leepector said he had servectone n Aire and the second and final notice would be served in due course. Dr. Ormsby had asked that necessary should be Jugs ; lie wished it to usett tmtobree npirdeetnrewtal.natn awnaysprri:aultledy (Dr. Ormsby) was u (the Inspector; had besindgonaellintbae qp ur st u wreayh,eactotdult,ll7 He ha superintended the drainage and some delay, had been caused through not having a local plumber. He had nothing to do with finding a local plumber. After be had served the final notice lie would see the owner per- sonally. FRODSIIANI WATER SUPPLY. The Local tiovernment 11, ard forwarded their for- mal sanction to the borrowing by the Rural Sanitary Authority of the Runcorn Union of the sum of £3.1300 for works of water supply lor the township of Prodaharn. •••hir. Williams iesial in connection with thus water it would not be undeairable to point out that while the Government bad been urging them . forward, and *Very local authority in the country, to proceed with such puhlic work as might be in contempla- tion, they had been perpectually held back by the action of the Local Government Board. It was two 'ran since they first approached the Lon.don this subject, and they had done all that was requested of them and finally au Inapector risme down to Prod- sham five months ago. The whoa.. of the cireunwit ;mores were pla..,ed before him, and lie (Mr. Williams) presuinesi he reported in due course. But they had *Mee lad to supply various items of Information to the Local Govern- merit Board ending with the visit of their , engineer and clerk to London last Thursilay. Ultimately by telegraph- ing they had succeeded lu gettiog a satiefactory reply. Maria& the summer they had had in Frodsham very mat scarcity of water, and what water they had, had been condemned by every medical man In the Ware both as to quantity and qual;ty. 'fhey had haul (In oomic of diptheric sore throat, and they had never been free from fever of one cleats or another, during the past six or eight months. Ile made this public statement so that the ratepayers amid those interested in the question might know that the delay had not been the Sault of the local authority. (Hear, hear.) The authority had done everything possi- ble. If this was the way the business of the country was carried on by the Local Government Board at an annual expenditure of hall a million pounds it was a bed job for the country. (Hear, hear.) fle was very glad to have received this sanction, and he should be sorry te make these remarks for any other purpose than simply to show that the very large expenditure which was going on in London, and the centralisation of Govern- ment, there was a wry prejudicial thing. (Hear, hear.) Government Timm •seems to be a concensus and the of opinion. that the Government Crisis. has' done the right thing at the right time in .offering. to mediate between mine- owners and. miners. There are, it is true, a .few dissentient voices. Bob the dissentients do not agree amongst themselves. Some say that the Government should have offered its good services at an earlier stage of the dispute; others are of , opinion.that in offering their services at all they are making a precedent which may have mischiev- ous results in-the future. But the general feeling undeubtedly is, as it has. been aptly expressed, . that the Government has chosen the " psychohogi- • cal moment 7—the very time wken it was to be expected that their intervention would bring to a close this grievous conflict. It shculd not be for- gotten by those who complain of dilatory action, that the government has no compulsory powers whereby to enforce its decisions on either play. Under the law as it now is, even the Cabinet can only confine its efforts to friendly mediation, to the work of smoothing over difficulties and irritat- ing' differences which inevitably arise when two ' contendingand antagonistic parties meet together. When the masters made a demand for a twenty- five per cent, reduction, and as long as they per- sisted in that demand, or anything approaching it, there was no room for the friendly offices of a mediator. Such terms could only be imposed upon the miners by defeat, complete and unequivocal. Lately, however, the points of difference between masters and men w ere comparatively trifling. The mine-owners had. receded from one position after another, and the men, on their side, displayed a conciliatory disposition. Matters having devel- oped thus far, there was clearly an opening for the friendly intervention of a third party of sufficient authority to secure the , respect and attention •of the whole ceuetry. In selecting Lord ROSEBBRY as mediator the Government made a choice which was in the highest degree satisfactory. A man of his connections was not likely to be accused of overlooking or treating with undue levity the just claims of capital, while, on the other hand-, he has on many occasions exhi- bited a quality, which is, unfortunately, very rare amongst men of his social standing—that of look- ing at labour questions from the point of view of the workman. Even this week, in a speech at the Colonia Institute, Lord ROSEBEICY has again given evidence of this quality ; for, when dealing with some criticisms that had been passed on the policy of Australian workmen with regard to Chineseirnmigration and other matters, be pointed out how much there was to be said in favour of that policy when you viewed things from the same standpoint as the roan who depends upon his weekly wage for a living. He admitted that in trying to keep out Chinese labourers the Austra- lian workmen were animated to some extent by selfish motives, but, he contended, it was not an unenlightened selfishness, and, at the worst, it was only a kind of selfishness which is by no means confined to the working classes. In addition to his other qualifieations Lord ROSZBERY has, as chairman of the London_ County Council and in other ways, had ample- experience in presiding over the debates of a mixed body of men. There- fore, if it be possible to bring the miners and the mine-owners into unison he is as likely as any man to succeed. To the few who seem disposed to argue against the Government interfering in any way hi indus- trial disputes, it may be said that a desperate disease needs a desperate remedy. And, besides, this is a struggle by which the general community are almost as much aflocted as the disputants themselves. In the present case the Government can fairly claim that it is acting for the best inte- rests of the nation. As week after week passi_d the stoppage more and more assumed the appear- ance of a monstrous contrivance for the enrich- ment of a few collif:ry-owners at the expense of the whole body of coal consumers and of unem- ployed workmen. We are told, upon the unjm- peachable authority of coal-owners themselves, that in the earlier' days of the lock-out magnificent profits were made from accumulated stocks, and now itis well understvd that the nett gains from some of the re-started pits may be reckoned by thousands of rounds in the week. NI hat has given the state of affairs a still more sinister aspect is the fact that in several eases Coal-owners haveppened some of their pits at the old rates, while 'others,are kept closed. It is possible that by this contrivance these coal-owners are making much higher profits than they would if all the . pits were at work, as they would then have to fulfil the cgntracts they have entered into.. If that be so, it is to ,be feared that some of the masters have becm.nder a ktiong ineb:cen ent not t come to terms too readily. j bolding out they made money, and if, in the end, they el forced a reduction of some kind upon the miners they w. n'd make more money. in the one case the public wavictimised,in the other the miners—and all, for the benefit of the mine-owners. Yet,there - are a few people who complain of Government interference. If the Jock-out had been much further prolonged the interference would have had to be of a more drastic character. Happily, the dispute is now at an end. The conference of mine-owners and miners was held yesterday, and after a prolonged discussion it was decided that the miners should resume work_ at the old rate of wages. This is, of course, a victory for the men.

labouring its way through the House of Com- mons, but oven if 'the Bill escapes the tender mercies of the House of Lords and becomes law, the British workman will still be behind his Ger- man brother in regard to insurance against sjek- ness,, accident, and old age. There are something like seven millions of German workmen insured against sickness. Of the contributions which pro- vide for this insurance, the employer pays one- third and the employed two-thirds, in return for his subscriptions the workman receives free medi- cal care and all appliances, besides an amount equal to one-half his wage as sick money for 13 weeks. For the insurance against accidents Ger- man employers have to find all the expenses. "The advantage to the labourer is the receipt of two- thirds hie wage in case of disablement. If only partially disabled, he receives such portion of his wage as is believed to measure his degree of help- lessness. If the accident results in death, twenty days wages are given as burial money, and to the widow twenty per cent, of the regular wage, - with fifteen per cent. to each child under fifteen years. The obligation is recognized to find work as far as possible for those injured in any business." It is said that both the sick law and the accident law are popu- lar in Germany and have "come to stay," but the scheme for old age pensions has not met with so much favour. We are not told of any. particular reason for this dissatisfaction, but it may be sur- mised that one of the reasons is that the benefits to the workman are too long deferred, seeing that the pension is not due till the completion of the seventieth year of age. And when the benefit does come it is not large, the average •pension never rising above forty-five dollars yearly. It is said that, on the whole, this German social legislation has been highly beneficial in its results. It gives hopefulness and a sense of security to those who are on the verge of poverty, and inspires in them the active energies of self help more tlian any • motives which spring from fear and disgrace.
SETTLEMENT OF THE DISPUTE.
