Edward Reddish, Stockton Hoath,was bra on remand before the Warrington magistrlV Monday on the charge of feloniously eml' ISO, the moneys of the Warrington Corp(' March last, and on divers other occasions. fendent pleaded guilty. The Town Clerk Lyon Whittle) prosecuted, and Mr.A. Br° \ fended.
ne Social Tai' first public meeting pro- Quebtions Union. rioted in Warrington by the

Social, Questions Union was a decided success. The Co-operative Ilan was, on Monday evening, crowded by an audience which was as enthusiastic and unanimous as the most sanguine member of the Union could desire. The meeting was, in its way, a very distinct testimony to the fact that, in .the opinion of a large body of the citizens of Warrington, there is a work for the Union to, do in the 'town. Those who were present were rewarded by hearing speeches which were, from beginning to e-d, on a high level, both as- to matter and manner. The admirable exposi- tion of the objects of the Union given by the Chairman,was marked by all Mr.MoNxs's clearness of a:ought and fairness of statement. ' It is re- ported in full on another page, and it may be read with advantage. We _venture ,to think that few will rise from its perusal without thinking that there is ample justification for the eitablishment of a Social Questions Union in Warrington, and that there is a wide scope for its beneficent acti- vity. . Mr. Mows, in our opinion, did well in laying much stress upon the urgent ' need for improving the dwellings of the poor in several parts of the 'town. If these veritable "plague spots" were improved out of existence a work Would have been done for which future generations of Warringtonians would have good reason to be thankful. As they staa they are a danger and a discredit to the town. It is, as Mr. Morms points out, the Town Council which should deal with these insanitary areas, and,indeed, the municipal authority isethe only body that has the powers requisite for such a task. The difficulties in the way are by no means slight, but they are not insuperable. If. the Town Council has the will it will find the way.

THE Government suffered a defeat Women's in the House of Commons on Thus- Suffrage. . day night.. It. was not of a serious nature, and they will easily survive it. As a mat- ter of fact, it was a rebuff administered by friends, and in .furtherange of what many staunch Liberals will consider a good cause. The Local Govern.- went Bill—better known as the Parish Councilsi Bill—was under discussion, and Mr. ,MoLAREN proposed an amendment in favour of enfranchis- ing all women. , married or single, who would be either on the Local Government or the Parlia- mentary register if they wore men. Mr. Fowrica has charge Of the Bill, and, naturally, he desires to getit passed through as expeditiously ahtl with as little contention as possible. Doubtless, he thought the amendment was about as full of con- tentious matters as an amendment well could be, and he declined to accept it. Mr. MCLAREN'S proposal found strong supporters in SLR CHARLES Dimen, Mr. STANSFELD, and, several other yell- known Parliamentarians who usually support the Government, and on a division it was carried by a majority uf twenty-one. The Opposition) of co,urse, voted with the dissentient Liberals. it is true, that there are many Conservatives opposed to the extension of women suffrage, but all through this Parliament the gentlemen who sit behind Mr. BALFOUR have shown a fine disregard of principle when there was a chance of damaging the Government. The incident, such as it is, is a very significant victory for women's suffrage, and 1 is a very distinct step in the direction of placing i women on an equality wio men in regard to poli- tical privileges.

div.p: OLIINTERR PRIZE SHOOTING AT NuirrOl. The annual prize meeting of the " G " Company (Newton), of the Prince of Wales Volunteers, outh Lancashire Regiment, took place on Saturday after- noon at the Higlifield Moss shooting range. The day was in every way favourable, the conditions ot light and wind, being altogether suitable for correct 'shooting, and as a consequence, 801110 very good scores were made. There was a large attendance of competitors, nearly the whole of the Company put- ting in an appearance. The arrangements at the range were carried out by a committee including Sergeant Instructor Wooding and the non-commis- sioned officers, and the meeting is considered to be the most successful that has been held. The chal- lenge cup presented by Mr. Thomas Molyneux, in 1886, was won by Sergeant J. Tunstall, and this Ong the third time he has secured, it now becomes his absolute property. At the conclusion of thel shooting, the competitors, assembled at the Gratin Hotel, Earlestown, for the purpose of receiving their prizes. Mr. Thomas Hamer, presided, and be was supported by Sergeant Instructor Wooding and Sergeant Dolan. The Chairman read the communication from Captain Widdowes in which that gentleman regretted his inability to be present to distribute the prizes owing to indisposition. Mr. Hamer, who is about to join the Company as lieutenant, then presented the prizes as under : Challenge cup, and money prize of 355., Sergeant Joseph Tunstall, whose scores were 25, at 200-yards, 33, 500 yards, total 58, 7 shots at each range; 2nd Corporal George Bailey, 305., 22, 34-56 ; 3rd, Col.- •7:ergeant M. McCoy, 255., 31, 18— 40; 4th, Sergeant James Tunstal, 219. 24, 24-48; sth, Sergeant W. Goodwin, 205., 23, 24-47 ; Bth, Sergeant B. Dolan, 13., 29, 18-47. The following also received prizes, Privates J. Powell, 46; S. Poulson, 41; Corporal G. Jacksan, 36 i.Lance-Sergeant M. Kenny, 36; Private W. L10yd,36 ; Lance-Corporal J. Poulson, 36 •, Cor- poral S. Roberts, 35 ; Private O. Williams, $4; J. Judson, 32 • Sergeant W. McCoy, 29; Private M. Flanagan, 29 ;Joseph Marsh, 29; J. Roberts, 28; T. Creed, 274 G. Travis, 23. Several priz s were also given to recruits, ranging in value from 103. to2s., the first prize being won by Private Scott. At tbe conclusion of the distribution the usual loyal toasts were honoured, also "The Captain," "Mr. Hamer and the future success of G. Company." A number of songs, &c., were given and the evening was enjoyably spent.

RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORSESPONDENT.

• On the initiative of Mr. Taylor, chairman of Run- corn Board of Commissioners, a fund has been commenced for the relief of the distress caused in Runcorn by the collier's dispute. Widnes has had a relief fund in existence for about ten weeks and there are hundreds who could scarcely have existed during that period but for its benificent operations, and it has occasionally been asked why something was not done for the poor in Runcorn, who ITe also prevented from working through no fault of their own. Fortunately Runcorn is not dependent upon one trade to the same extent as Widnes and the pinch has not been felt so keenly. There are some who even at present argue that there is no need for a relief fund, but there can be little doubt that there are many families keenly suffering at present. 'there is always a certain class of the population. who, whenever such funds are started will clamour for a portion,no matter what their.oircumstances, but those who are frequently most in ;need, lave to be searched out and helped almost in spite of them- selves. It is for this latter class, no,cloubt, that Mr. Taylor has taken action, and thatt the appeal for donations is made.

At last there is a prospect of Fredsham obtaining an aeequate and a pure supply of water. The Local Guverninent Board have sanctioned the-borrowing of a sum of £3BOO for the purpose orcarrying out the scheme propounded by Metiers. Timmins the water engineers of Runcorn, who have made a liv- ing on the Marsh near the Gels Weeks and obtained sn excellent result. Neary nine swaths of valuable time have been wasted through the-deliberate not to say slow manner in which the Local .Gov,rninent Board have moved in the matter, alui Mr. Williams gave utterance to a few well deserved words of' couidemnation at the meeting of the Rural Sani- tary Committee on Tuesday last. It is a matter for surprise that in affairs of the utunist sanitary importance there slisuld so frequently be danger- ous delays through the circuinloce.tion of the Government department.

The decisive step taken by the Beard of Com- missionerS in determining to proceed with the erection of the Institute, although the whole of the money needed was not in hand, has revived the in- terest in that institution. The prediction made by Mr. Wiswail that the money would 4peedily be torthcoming, seems likely to be fully .verified. At a meeting of the General Committee, held on Mon- ody night, under the presidency of that gentleman, the following promises were made: Mr. F.J. Nor- man, C. 59;. Mrs, S. Taylor, .CSO4 Mr. Merman, £5 ; Mr. W. Ilandley, £5; Mr. W. Ilankinson. .d 5 Mr. U. -J. Griot>, £5; Mr. Bawlinson, £5; Mr. John Holt, ..C2; and Mr. Moston undertook to raise .£5. it was Heckled that collecting books should be prepared and distributed, and it was further resolved to re- present to the Board of Commiscioners Alfet the balance needed to erect the Institute free from debt, %conk,' probably be raised aud urge them to.proeeed •with the work at once.

At the Ailchrist Jecture on Ther3rnry• night, D. Wilsou, after a highly interesting lee? are made an loquent reference to the propolied Lustitute and to the beneti:g that would result frai . the atudy of „eientitic &object, even when undettalwn a a mental exercise. without hope or gain. Iris remarks art, well worth rending.

div.p: THE EX ;NIINEP, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 18-, 1893.
GILCHRIST LECTURES AT RUNCORN.
TUE TECIINICAL INSTITUTE.

The fourth of the series of Gilchrist lectures was held in Runcorn Public Hall on Thursday night to a large audience. The subject was "The heart and the story of the circulation," and DeAndrew Wilson P.R,S.E., F.LS. &e. was the Lecturer. Mr. S. Taylor, Chairman of the Board of Com- missioners presided and in opening the proceedings he said Canon Wood, Mr. Wiswall and Dr. Gastaldi had given very elaborate descriptions of the object of the lectures, that there was nothing for him to say in reference to it,but he might state that these lectures had alreadyhad a wonderful effect in promoting the Technical Institution. On Monday night they had a meeting of Commissioners and outsiders and he was pleased to see a number of working men there, and in the room tat night £llO was promised. (Applause.) It was announced that there were twelve months to raise the money re- quired and he was highly pleased that one working man promised to give £2 himself and to collect £5 more it he had a book (applause.) Another working man also volunteered to collect £5 or £lO, whilst yet another , suggested that a number of workmen of Runcorn should have books, and said he felt sure that a large sum could be raised by them amongst their fellow workmen. The Technical Institute was for the benefit of the working people and if they would only take an interest in the subject there was not the least doubt of it being brought to a successful issue. The shillings, sixpences, and pennies of the working men of Runcorn were more appreciated by him than a pound been one who could well afford to give it, and if a hundied workingmen would take a book and each one collect £5 in the twelve months that would be £5OO. He understood that some workingmen had got an idea that the institute was in- tended for those who could well afford to pay for their children's education. This was not so. The building would be open principally for the working classes, and he, was sure no working man's sons or daughters would Ibe refused the facilities it would afford. After this 'course of lectures had concluded it was intended to invite the workingmen to a public meetingand he hoped they would attend. Be felt sure that these lectures had done a great deal to help forward the movement for building the Institute and he hoped that next year they would be able to approach the GolchristTrustee.s and say " Now we have got the building. we want you to help us again. (Applause.) And he felt sure the Trustees would not hesitate to give them another treat. (Loud !applause.) The Lecturer, after explaining what was meant by the word circulation, said two thousand years ago men knew nothing about the circulation of the blood,and the man who made the discovery of the. circulation was Wm. Harvey, a celebrated and distinguished English. , man. The heart was a hollow muscle,and as muscle was flesh, if they referred to the heart as a hollow muscle, they truant that it consisted of the same sort of steff as the flesh of the body. The heart was a muscle which con- tracted, and when it became smaller it forced the blood out along the different channels through which it had to go. The Lect.irer then proceeded to describe the heart, in lower life, and remarked that the human heart had the same structure as that of every bird and quadruped. The microscope enabled them to distinguish betwoa the blood of quadrupeds, fishes,frogs, reptiles,and birds, but it Was ii1.1110(ht impossible Id slistinguish human blood trom ..eadruDeCl. They could tell the diffe- rence between the blood of a marl and ttleTiood of a He admitted that there were differences, but they cou., .not tell them under the microscope. Continuing, the Lecturer narrated how the heart was ditided into two complete sides the right and left sides, and that each side was divided into two chambers a smaller or upper chamber called the auricle, and a lower and larger chamber, the ventricle. Having explained why the heart was thus a double organ, Dr. Wilson pointed out that there were two circulations,the pulmonareaor that through the lungs, and the systemic, or that through the body. He further etated that the arteries carried pure blood from the heart to the body, and the veins carried impure blood Irons the body to the heart and lungs. These arteries and veins were con- nected by capillaries. The Lecturer described the different valves of the heart, how they acted in regulating the flow of blood, and also the way in which the nerves checked and spurred the heart. In concluding his lecture Dr. Wilson said the Gilchrist Lectures were always given in aid of some projector another, and in Runcorn they were intended to aid the erection of the Technical Institute. Ile had nothing, as a stranger specially to say about that except in a gen- eral sense.' Even, the comic papers nom-a-days were taking up the cry about almost everyarticle we purchased being made in Germany or in Austria or 13.1eium, never made in England. When he purchased a glass for his reading lamp, a glass .which generally broke at the second time of using (laughter) he was always tempted to ask " Why made in Germany; why not made in England:" The reason was not far to seek. It was because Germany had gone ahead in this so called Tech- nical education ; and at last those responsible for the education of this country had awakened up to that feet. In the district of Runcorn they depended upon a techni- cal industry closely associated with chemical science,and it would be the suprenicst folly in them to educate the rising generation ia their trade by the old rule of thumb, vrithout underet teeing the theory and the scien- tific practice of it. He took it that the Tech- nical Institute would be the practical application of science to train the workman and to keep him abreast In his information of the latest science of the day a-id to place him where every British workman ought to be, on a level and on a par with the workmen of foreign coun- tries who were being trained in these technical matters. (Apt lause.) He could appreciate to the full, the great work which the people oh Runcorn intended to do and understand why each working-man was invited to give a helping hand. Ile cordially wished a:1 success to the Institute which would represent a powerful adult :fie factor in their midst. If this course of lectures had in any sense contributed to the greater success of lhat noble work amongst them, he was quite certain that bth the trustees and the lectorers would feel that their lab air had net -been in vain. (Applause.) Dr. Wilson con- tinued to say that the study of science, without any technicalsogical end, was interes.ing, elevating and instructive and he looked upon the idea of in- teresting the general public in popular science not less an important work of tire Gilchrist Trust than that of interesting them in technicalogy at have, for science bad a certain leveling influence upon the people all arouni. We lived in a beautiful world, well worth studying, that formed part of a still greater universe, 'and we ought tokn.w something about the universe in which we lived, and these Gilchrist lectures ought to stimulate them to get hold of a little science and add to their lives a new interest. The difference between one man and another in this world was not riches. Evers. man Jack of us lived in a rut. The first man spent the whole of his life in a rut, the second man tried ts get his head a little above his daily toil and saw something, of the blue sky beyond. We had all got our grinding work, of life to do ; some of us with wiil4 aims and aspira- tions, others with very commonplace aims, hut whether great aims or commonplace, let isa all get some little Study outside our daily grind work, and ft would take the mind off our toil and make las more liberal in our views, more charitably disposed t iwards our fellowmen and give us greater and grander conceptions of the universe of which we formed a part. Get some little study of their own scientifically, think over it, read about it. Literature was cheap, even the newspapers were foil of science,and life would have at length'. one additional interest for them ; that perhaps it had not before the Gilchrist lec- tures. (Applatfse ) He urged them with all the power at his command to engage in mental study and it might be that like David carrying loaves to camp toiled a throne, like Saul seeking his father's asses and becotnine, King of Isreel, so they • in their more simple •science study expecting nothing at all would find a mental com- fort and an intellectual heritage, which no inciden life could lesson. that widish no misfortune of exists colds' ever take away. (r.ond and prolonged ap- please.) A vote of thanks was accorded to both lecturer and chairman. The lecture was beautifully illustrated by a lantern manipulated by Mr. Ernest Garbuts.
SERVING A DItITNEEN MAN WITH BEER, AT LYMM.
A PUBLICAN CONVICTED.

Yesterday afternoon at LymmTetty Sessions, Mr. 'l'. P. Norris in the chair, a publican named Wm. Hill, keeper of Ole Spread Eagle Inn, Lymm, was charged with supplying Richard Oakes with drink, when he was already drunk. Mr. A.Browne. Warrington, represented the defendant. t•iergeaut Garner, said at 4-20 on the 23rd of October, be was on duty on Lyruna Bridge, when he saw a man named Richard Oakes, come from the direction of Heatley. He vim; very drunk. About ten minutes afterwards he (witness) was greatly surprised to see Oakes in the Spread Eagle Inn, drinking a glass of beer. He asked the publican whether he didn't think the man had had enough drink, to winch the publican replied he had, and took the remaining portion of the beer from the man, and threw it in the wash bowl, and gave the man his money back. He also told the man to go nome, and no to come into his house again. The publican ad- mitted serving the man and said, " Do your duty Garner." Cross-examined by Mr. Browne, witness said he didn't see the man go Mt° the Millstone Inn after- wards. Mr. Browne said it was not necessary to call other witnesses on behalf of the prosecution, as his client admitted that the man was drunk. The man had hardly got the beer in his hand when the officer came in, and Mr. Hill had served him witliout examining him carefully. He quite admitted that it was within the letter of the law that an offence had been committed He was not going to contend that there should not be a conviction in that case, but he would say this, that it was one of those offences no publican could help. The man came in, and the landlord, on the spur of the moment, and in the dark, served him. The magistra GCS fined the defendant Is, and costs, but did not endorse the licenie.

Win. Oakes wa3 next charged with having on the 23rd October' been drunk on the premises of the Spread aigle Inn. Defendant pleaded not guilty. Sergeant Garner proved the case, arid the InAgistrates fined de- fendant 23. 61. including costs.
TRIAL OF THE NEW FIRE ENGINE.

Yesterday morning a semi-lsublic trial was made of the capacities of the new fire engine "Captain," purchased by the Corporation of Warrington from Messrs. Merry weather and Sons, Greenwich. The place selected for the trial was Messrs. Fairclougls's Mills, Howley, that being the highest building in the town, and there being the additional advantagel Of an ample water supply. Lie fire brigade turned out about 10-30 and under the command of thiper-1 intendeut Turner, took charge of the new steam fire engine. Die engine was followed to Mersey Mills, by two wagonette loads of Corporation officials, Town Councillors, and friends. Amongst them were Councillor Hutchinson, Chairman of the Fire En- gins Committee, and after whom the engine has been named, Alderman Ashton, and Councillors Dr. Cannel', Shillcock, Muir, Smethurst, Shaw, Garner, and Hilbalso Dr. Gornall and -Inspector Norman. Mr. J. Longdin superintended the trial on behalf of the Corporatiou, whilst the experiments were carried out by Captain .I. H. Cleaver, the makers' representative, and the engine was worked by the Company's engineer, Mr. Harper. • The experiments at the mill proved the engine to be quite dasiable of the Weak guaranteed. Four jets were used and the water was thrown out in a way that at once gave all satistaction in connectian with the mechanism of the machine. The quantity of water issuing from the jets per minute was 590 gallons, being 10 gallons above the quantity guaranteed, and in 8 minutes, 45 seconds, 100.bs. of sl.eam were got up, being the record time and quantity. The mills from the ground to the top of the chimney are 150 feet high, and above their summit from a 1 inch jet, water was thrown 10 feet the full pressure of 110Ibs being then on the steam gatig.e. The highest building in the town is 80 feet so that there is no estab- lishment, which if •it took fire, would be beyond the range of the new engine. In the force of ater tho engine, when worked by steam, is capable of throwing Out quite four dines the quantity emitted from the jets of the hydraulic engines. The test at Howley was coin- pleted by twelve o'clock when the engine, followed by the party, was driven to the Town Hall. Here a large number of the public gathered to witness the experi- ments, which on this occasion were meant, not to test the mechanism of the engine, but the capacities of the water mains. It was discovered, however, that the eight inch mains will not yield, without pump:ng, anything like the amount of water required ti keep the engine at full pressure. Consequently before the volume of 590 gallons could be produced from the jets, connecti.ins had to be made with two water mains, one of Aptileton and the other of Winwiek water. With one main in uso the water tank could only be filled a little more than half. With the working ,of the, ensine the -Borough Surveyor and Captain Hutshinson, together with the other officials, expressed their completesatisfaction. The experiments tatd for ab ut ast Inns, after which the party partook of liinc.heon in the Mayor's parlour. eat fwo o'clock in the al torn on the party ateemblel in Wilson-Fat ten-street to witytese_th.4 t riaJ of tticeanm fam's hydranifc sewer nusinirs Tabs is a novel eontriv• slice for washing the whole interior suifac, s of the sewers and drains by means of water Hs at fire englie pressure. The apparatus consists of a tube fitted a ills a number of small n zz!es and is connected by means of hose to a steam Dumping engine or other high pressure water supply. The tube is mounred on four 7 heels. and closed at the forward and a ring being fitted, by which it can be drain from manhole to manhole in the sewers, the hose being paid out from the surface as reqnfred,a ith the pressure of 501bs. and upwards,the whole interior of the pipes er culverts is thoroughly cleansed in a manner that cannot be approached by the usual method of flushing. The efficacy of the " flusher." greatly im- pressed itself on the party at inspection. It proved effec- tive in the removal of debris and accumulated comnost- tion in the sewers, which the present system of flushing has failed to touch. By the present system a cost of slx shillings is often incarreil in flushing a sewer, but by the flusher it is considered the cost can be reduced to one-half.

div.head: WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. I
div.p: WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. I

At the weekly meeting of the Widnes (T. P. O'Connor) Branch Irish National League held in the League Rooms, St. Paul's Buildings, Victoria-road, on Sunday, there was a very large attendance. Councillor Hugh O'Donnell, president, was in the *hair. After the usual routine business had been gone through, the reading of a paper, postponed from a previous date, was given by Mr. David James, of Appleton, entitled " Why am I a member of the Irish National League." Mr. lames, who reads in a calm cool manner, every word being clear and distinct, said in the first place the League was a legal soci,ty or band cf man working together in a legal way for the accomplishment of cettain objects as stated on their cards of member- ship, viz :—To assist in the attainment of that form of self government -.altiels is desired by the majority of the Irish people both at home and abroad. And, in pasing, might he ask "Did the Home Rule Bill of Mr. Gladstone come up to the desired standard of the Irish Nation?" He believed they would answer "yes," although he for one did not consider it a perfect Bill but only a step in the right direction in which their Irish Nationalist members of Parliament had carried out their part nobly with the Liberals of Great Britain. Greater fidelity, a higher sense of honour, a more eager willingness ta make per- sonal sacrifice for the common cause, could not have brin shown by any men. Here was an object lesson as to what might be expected from Dome Rule. Those who had shown such loyalty and discipline in the pro- longed and trying struggle of the past session would not lae found wanting,. in similar virtaes when they represented a nation which had acquired, within well defined limits, tLe right of mlnaging its own affairs. Mr. O'Elogan proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. James, which was seconded by Councillor J. Gough, who in a few well- chosen remarks punted out the necessity for united action among the Nationalist workingtnen of Widnes,and hoped that if the Widnes Branch I.N L. continued to flourish as it had done within this last y ear ' they would shortly see it having a building of its own. Mr. John Campbell. supported the vote, which was carried unanimously.
THE 31AYOlt OF WIDNES AT CEIURCH.

'• The annual Mayoral visit to Church, took place at ' Widnes, on Sunday, when his Worship was accom- panied by the Corporation, members of the School Board, the Relief Committee, and other gentlemen, to St. Paul's Church. The procession from the Town Hall was headed by Gos-age's Band, then came Mr. Whittle, the Town Hall attendant, bearing a wand, with the Mayor (Alderman Gassage) and the Town Clerk (Mr. 11, S. Oppenheim), attired in their robes, immediately behind. Then came Aldermen El. S. Timmis and J. 14 illiamson, Councillors Barlow, Shuttlewortli, Christie, Millough, Langton, G. 1. Neil, Davies, Owens, Quin% Singleton, Shores,' Gough, Caruey, W. W. Go sa e,T. Smith, D. Wright, and O'Donnell ; Messrs. B. Brown, F. 11. Pankhurst, T. Hartland, S. R )biuson,- F, Neil, B. Bort hvvick, W. Farraut, C. Hemingway, W. PaJin, T. Showell Bedrock, T. Craik (assistant clerk), S. Hoyle (ac- countant), I. Carr (engineer), J. S. Sinclair (sur- veyor), C. 11. Lewin, J. Woodend,W, Lowe, C. Whit- field, T. Hughes, T. Peters, and J. M. Dale. Behind the. Corporation offieials walked the fire brigade in uni- torah sua the rear v.,a2 beenght up hty a number of the local vacenteers, unuer comtuauu Les. Tim polica under the command of .9uperinttridget Eei:hley and luspecter Pattluson, I.4treed giiard. On the pro. cession arriving at the &lurch door, the Catholic mem- bers of the Council fell cut and went to their own place of worship. The sacred edifice was crowded to excess, and hundreds had to be refused admission. The service was conducted by the Rev. W. Stanton Jones, curate, and the Rev. W. flalgson, M.A., vicar, preached from the text, " Righteousness exaltetli a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people." - (Proverbs xiv., 34.) The preacher descri tad the" Mayor's Sunday" as an admir- able institm ion being as it were, the trwifs recognition of Almighty God. The words ot the text ought to he inscritßA on every assembly senate hoese, and council chamber. Sin had been tle c 'use of the decline or destruction of nutty nations. If England as a nation gave way to had greed, drunkennesa and gambling,then she would have to piv the nmalty. We gloried in our cominerc,, our sold era, and our sacra, hut the best bulwark of a nation was righteousness. And a nation's righteousness depended upon each individual. What was it that at, into the righteousn,st of a nction. Per. hapi the first thing that would strike them was " class hatred," Here in w Rifles they were breught to the very verge of starvation through no fault of their own, but simply because the miners and owners could not are. Why should there be this war between labour and capital They were supplementary one to the other and ought to be the greatest friends. They wanted a better under- standing between class and ChM, and the teaching of Jens Christ inculcating into society. They wanted a fair day's work for a fair day's wags, and vice versa There must b- more conscience in the labour question, and a recognition of the brotherhood of man. The preacher also dealt with other aspects of his text. The collection which was in aid of the distress fund realised £40,. At the conclusion of the service, the National Anthem was sung.and Gassages bawl played the "Halle- lujah Chorus " art-votive: arzyr.— •

On Monday evening, the annual public meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. James Handley, J.l'. The CLERK said that the discussion upon the Parish Councils Bill was a very interesting and instruc- tive one. There was one general feeling which seem-id to pervade the meeting and in fact, the country iu gvn- era! which was that the Poor LAW Guardians had done their duty so well, and that the decrease of pauperism, and expenditure in relief was of so ma 'lced is character that it would be impossible to substitute for the guar- dians a body more useful tor the duties imposed upon tip mby the law. This feeling prevailed All over the country and no one seemed to take exception to it, and It was on that account that very gr,at pressure wis being brought to hear upon the Government and Parlia- ment to sere rate the Poor LAW altogetior [rein the Parish Councils Bill. WARRINGTON DRAMATIC SOCIETY.
"THE MONEY SPINNER."

Of the many successes-which -have attended the rather unfrequent public performances of the War- rington Dramatic Society, none can be described as more complete than those of Wednesday and Thurs- day evenings. After having withheld from public scrutiny for a considerable period its admieable combination of histrionic talent, the society came forth on the two evenings mentioned to perform the " Money Spinner." The object of the performances was to raise a sufficient sum to wipe off the exist- ing debt on the Gymnasium, a debt which hampers the managers of that admirable Institution in their I endeavours to develop its usefulness. The large audience which attended the initial performance I included, in addition to friends of the Society and ! the institution, a large gathering of the elite of the ! neighbourhood, and it is fair to surmise from the substantial nature of the proceeds, that just as the performances from an artistic point of .view gave every satisfaction,they would be equally gat!fying from a Pecuniary stand point. One of the most noticeable and admirable featurei of the performance, was theapposite and highly artistic character of the proscenium. It was representative of a tastefully arranged drswirag-room, and in every detail of design and decoration reflected credit upon the artistic abilities of Mr. j. Hesketh, who generously contributed the work as a portion of los assistance in the cause. By the aid of this excellent stage property, augmented by furniture lent by Mr. 'l'. Sutton, the stage manager, Mr. John E. Davies, demonstrated the value of his experience and his capacity to direct and arrange the various scenea„ and stage pictures which add to the realism of the stories which the actors had I as their task to unfold. On Wednesday evening, Mr. Pmero's entertaining comedy was preceded by the some- what lengthy nine "Fref zing a Mother-in-law." This laughable gem is ufficiently well-known to render needless a resume of the plot for the guidance of the reader. 'the female characters in it were impersonated by Miss Dora Collas and Miss Schofield, both members of icaaing Liverpool Dramatic Societies. But it is hard to !Fay which of the ladies merited the most praise—Miss 'Schofield for her /quip itbetic and • clever realization of the whimsical " Mrs. Watrnuff," or Miss Collas for her portrayal of the decorous " Miss Emily IVatmuff," wino loved aga'reit her mother's w:sh. In the male characters, Mr. Alfred Woods as the henpecked "Mr. Watmuff," stood out in protninerit excellence. His "mike up" was superb, his natural way of bringing out the laughable mannerism of a perverted and perverse "old croney," cempleted a delineation which compared with any of Mr. Wood's excellent impersonations. Then much cre- dit was due to Mr. T. J. Mils., for his capital " Walter Litherlind," and t) Mr. G. It. Williamson, for an inter- pretation of the fortune-hunting "Ferdirand Smith," into which part be infused an easy and befitting non- chalance.

The performance of the" Money Spinner" may be said in general to have attained the acme of excellence. To any( e' with a personal knowledge of the artistes, it was obvi ms that they had been chosen for their tasks with a due regard for fitness, The story is a simple one, tieing illustrative of the danger a good natured clerk named Harold Boycott has run, in drawiog upon his employes banking accounts to assist a brother out of misferture. Being snspected of the defalcations he is watched, by a detective named" Jules Faubert," who is I employed as a fellow clerk and who manages to ingra- tiate himself into Boycett's family. . Tile day before the accounts are to be met, " Lord Kengusaie," a former lover of "Mrs. Boycott," and her tester's fiancee, visits the house. "Mrs. Boycott "in her extremity to save her husband, resorts to a game at cards with the nobleman, and being the daughter of an old gambler succeeds in cheating until her " little game," is denounced by the detective. Tiiis leads tc a " scene "which is erel el by Kengusaie, in admiration of his old " fla me," generously helping her husband out of the difficulty. The character of Boycott was imperson- ated by Mr. A. Browne, who had in Miss Cones, a sup. porter, whose "lines "contained more feeling and mos tlon, genuinely given, than any other character. Then there was "Dorinda Croodle,"—thelatter'e vivacious sis- ter—and Lord Kengussie's affanced, a part which was depicted with a piquancy very creditable lc Miss Schofield. :But the principal character of the piece, the heart and soul of it, in fact, was " Baron Croodle," the " brandy-nipping, " lugubrious, retired o!d gaming- house keeper, father-in-law to Boycott. In this Mr. A. Woods evinced successfully the gift he possesses of depicting the whimsicalities of the " older generation," But it was a theme of common comment whether as the simp!e, kindhearted, noodle, " Lord Kengussie." Mr.II. IV. Cookson, did not score a success equal to that won by Mr. Woods. In tine-last act,where, half reproachfully, half indignantly, he admonishes his grief-stricken Tomer lover, " for cheating at love two years ago, and now at cards," Mr. Cookson introduced so much true fe.eliag, that on both nights, the , scene roe-rived the loudest applause of any in the play. Mr G. T. Brundrett's "Jules Faubert " was an excellent impersonation of a somewhat thankless part and Mrs. Kewley deserved ample credit for her " Margot, the French waiting &I," whilst Mr. J. T. Picton, as "porter" stayed a re,- arneunt of solidit:

, crs-playeta • Ui Thins lass ovanintluk Mon.,p-Rpherina mandayse.-- e,echied be the-comedietta "Uncle's Will." This proved a mire enirt t tining farce than that of the previaus and nanFlsted almest entlrely of amusing by-play between a pair of lovers. These two characters were imperson- ated by Mr. C. If. Wood (Charles Castimorr), and Miss Collas (Floienco Marigold). The latter gave another •:•arripte of her adt&raWe verratility in the emol ional parts whilst he ru: ma displayed quite an ea ceptional amount of naturalism in delineating the vac cillating passions of love and jealousy or the ch meter. As the eccentric old 'guardian," Mr. Barker," Mr. 11. W. Cookson augmented .the credit won by his other Impersonation. The "Money Spinner " went off with all the first night defects remedied, and when the curtain fell the vociferous applause of the audience could only be appeased by Cie reappearance of the artistes and stage manager bAore :..he footlights. Much of the credit of the success of the performances can ba claimed by the very able orcher.ra whose services were gratuitously given, and whose performances were a pleasing change daring the intervals between the acts. The orchestra was under the leadership of Mr. R. 11. Pearson, and consisted of the following w..1!-kolown Ideal instrumentalists :—Messrs. J. Ribeita, A. Knowles, M. Foster, J. Bilverton, J. Burrows, U. Bond, W. Chatmck, W. Podmore, J. Ilipkiss, and %V. Waterfield.

Perhaps a word about the history of the Society would not he uninteresting. It was formed about 40 years ago by Mr. Joseph Davies. It was then a " Reading Society" awl was a branch cf the Old Trafford Dramatic Society. It numbered a meg its members such local notables as the late Captain Ileynoldi, Maiir Pickmere, and Alder- man Harrison. Some time afterwards the Society was converted into a Dramatic Society through the instru- mentality of Mr. J. D. Picton, and Mr. J. E. Davies, an of the founder, who succeeded his worthy fattier in the aims of stsgc manager and presi tent. The Society for many years used Only to give one performance anuually the proceeds of which were devoted t the Infirmary, and that they were of a substantial character may be sur- mised from the fact that it was an agteement made between the donors and the recipents, that the moneys should be invested as a special item of Income. From the tittle the Public Hall changed bands and became a theatre, the Society has appeared in public only twice. and on one of those occasions it was to perform in aid of the funds of the School of Art. This broke the old cus- tom of only assisting one institution and the Gymnasium Committee taking advantage of the precedent, applied for similar assistance, and received it from the perform- ances of Wednesday sad Thursday. The older mmabers .1 the company win took part, are all able amateurs, arid were especially assisted by' Mr. T. E Davies, the stage manager, and Mr. A. Woods, whose 18 years con- nection with the Society give bins souse claim to the, ap- pclation of " veteran." Th,- four ladies af 10 took tart, the Misses Cans, Miss Sehofield aid Mrs. Kewley, are amateurs of considerable note in Liverpool.

div.p: sadly neglected for many years, until our worthy pre- sident set an example that I hope this association will follow. If we could find out how many of our Blue Coat Schools lads after leaving Behead have taken up the pro- fession, we should be surprised to think that with all their training there should be so few who are known musicians. The reason is this: there has been no one to create any interest. Our Musical Society has failed to make a single instrumentalist, and it is left for this association to work out some scheme that will assist to bring our townto 'such a standard that it will be second to none for giving a musicAl education to her sons who have the gift and talent for music. If we have our sculptors and artists I fail to see why we cannot have a musician." (Applause.) Mr. Taylor, continuing, said the 307 that he had mentioned as belonging to the assoc- iation did not give an idea of the number of instrument- alists in Warrington, who numbered upwards of 500. Jf the members of the association would only stick together they would make a name for themselvee that they shou.d all be proud of in days to come. (Applause.) The President expressed his pleasure at hearing such a satisfactory report, and he attributed the prosperity of the society in a large Measure to the admirable manner in which the secretary, Mr. Taylor, had worked. Ue had worked very hard for the association from its forma- tion, and he (the President) could baldly have believed that Mr. Taylor was a man of such enthusiasm. (Hear, hear.) The report was adopted. ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

Mr. T. J. Down, was unanimously re-elected presi- dent, and the following vice-presidents were elected The Mayor(Alderman E.Greenall),Councillors ll. Roberts, Heaton, Cannel!, Bolton, and F. IV. Monks, and Messrs. F. Monks, J.P.,C.C.,A. H. Crosfield, It A. Naylor, and T. Morris. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle was re-elected treasurer and Mr. J. Taylor the secretary.

div.head: PRESENTATION.
div.p: PRESENTATION.

This completed the official buSlneSs, the PRESIDENT. then said he had been teispnest,d to present to their Secre- tary a memento of the appreciation of the Association. The memento, he alluded to, was a beautiful walnut inlaid writing case. In making the presentation he said he had known Mr. Taylor for a very considerable time 1 and he could truly say he had never known anything but good of him. (Applause.) He did not know where else the Association would have found such an excellent secretary as they had found in Mr. Taylor, to whose Praiseworthy efforts was due much of the prosperity of the Association. (Applause.) tie hoped Mr. Taylor would live long to continue his excellent endeavours in the interests of music in the town. (Applause.) Mr. TAYLOR in responding expressed tne gratitude with which he accepted such a kind token of apprecia- tion. lie then made some brief allusions to the difficul- ties which had been encountered in working up the Asenciation. div.p: WEEKLY ItEPour ON TuE HEALM OF WARRINGToN

During the week, which was the 45th of the current year, the following births and deaths were registered :—Births : Warrington, 44 ; Latchford, 6 ; total,so. Deaths : Warrington.lB ; Latchford, 1 ; total 19. The excess of births over deaths was 31. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 179 per .1.000, against 19 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 211 the corresponding week of last year. The death-rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 1.7 per 1,000, against 3.6 the average rate of the four previous weeks, and against 7.6 the corresponding week of 1892. The ages of mortality were :-0 to 1, 10 ; 1 to 5,4; 5 to 15.0; 15 to 25, 0 ; 25 to 60, 3; 60 up 2 ; total, 19. The deaths included 1 from whopping comfit ; 1 from diarrhoea ;1 from acute rheumatism; 2 from premature birth : 5 from fling disease; 5 from brain disease ; 3 from heart disease. The following cases of infectious disease have beon reported during the week:— scarlet fever, 7; enteric fever, 1. ETEOIIOLOGY.- The mean temperature was 382 Fah., and therefore 4 deg. colder than the preceding week. The ' mum temperature 47 F.,was recorded on the sth inst. and the minimum temperarurd 23 F., on the 15th inst. The rainfall measured .09 inch. The general direction was N.-E., the reading of the Anemometer tenoting 970 miles.—JouN El. GORNALL. Sledicel Officer of Health.

_ _ AT WARRINGTON. Mr. Reginald Owen, junr., is 1! "..:y particular fellow indeed, and as a mNI 4 the Warringtonem Board of Guardtans, he Will halm everything said and done in pfoper order. At the meeting of the B lard last. Wednesday, Mr. ir,titcliffe the chairman, was giving particulars of the poor-law conference recently held in London, which he attended in com- pany with the Vice-Chairman and the Clerk, lie lied fairly launched in his story, when Mr. Owen suddenly got upon his legs and asked the Chairman, whether he had been to the conference. " Yes " said the chairman in amazement," I m telling you my experiences there." "I am sure you did not tell us you went," retorted Mr. Owen, "you said that the Vice-Chairman and the Clerk were there, but you net., r said that you were there als Mr. Ratcliffe repeated that he did say so, and asked how he could tell them about the conference if he had not been present. " Well " said the big junior "I i never heard you, verhaps I hare an infirmity." He then subsided. The chairman had by -Ana time lost the thread of his story, but after a little delay, be pro- ceeded without any more interruption.

The me •ting held in the Co-operative ITall, on M mday night, under the auspices of the Social Questions Union was a great success. A more 'en- thusiastic meeting has not been held in Warrington, for some time, and it showed as the !ley. F. C.. Aked said,that a Warrington audience is as capable of taking as gre it an interest in the eauie of social( purity 48 the people ot other towna are; That councillors Relieri's Elation at the election of Alder- men Ashton was endorsed by a large number of• people was well evidenced by the prolonged cheer- ing which greeted the Rev. John Yenges allusion to that incident, and also by 'in reception given to the Councillor himself when he rose to speak.

The deputation from Liverpool MS an excellent. One. The Her. S. R. Armstrong as the elder of the two gave Fome very pod and sound advice and urged the Warrington people to follow the example• - of the Liverpool people with regard to the drink party. The Rev. C. F. Akefl, however, came wit first favourite. That ha is such a powor in Liver- pool will occasion no surprise to those who heard his speech on Monday tight. Ile has all the. requirements of the °rater, such as a ;read voice, fluency of speech, freedom of action, and also humour and fire. Needless to say, lie took the people by storm, and should he ever come to Wax. rington again, he would be certain of an inmenso gathering.

I am glad to note that the Rev. J. Kinlan bas • now so tar recovered from his sudden and serious - attack of illness 04 he expects to preach in Bold- street Chapel to-morrow evening. div.p: THE COIIMON LOT.

However differently situated as regards social posi- tion, or separated as regards location, it. is the common Lot of all sorts and conditions of men to be liable to various ailments and diseases. All men under these circumstances are, to a certain extent, placed on the same footing. "A fellow-feeling makes us wondrous kind," and nothing interests a sick man more than to hear the experience of others who have suffered from the same complaint as himself. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

DISTURBING DIVINE SERVICE. Thomas S. Williamson (13) 242 Liverpool-road,William John Lea (12) 303, Liverpool-road, and Ernest Seed (11) 129, Liverpool-road, were each brought before the War- rington magistrates on Monday on the charge of riotous behaviour on November Sth,during, divine service at St. Luke's Church.—P.C. Turner said that he received instructions to Watch about St. Luke's Church on the above date. While there, he saw the three boys shout outside of the church,knock at the door and also 'bang" the handle of the door, during service time. He caught Lea and got the names ot the other two.—The Rev. H.J. Wild, curate in charge said that he was very sorry to have to make complaints, but there was snch a great amount of annoyance that he was compelled to report the matter. Ile wished the bench to deal leniently in this case. The Chief Constable said that there were con- tinued complaints from a Roman Catholic Church, and a Wesleyan chapel concerning the same thing. The mag- istrates dismissed the defendants with a caution. BRUTAL ASSAULTS ON WOMEN. At the Borough Court on Wednesday, two cases for assaults on women were heard. William Ashton, Rose and Crown-st., was charged with assaulting amlbeating Mrs. Samson, a married woman, on Saturday night. The complainant's evidence showed that she was going down Rose and Crown-st. about 10.30 on the day in question when the prisoner got hold of her and refused to let her go away. He pulled her to the ground and kicked her in the face, causing two black eyes. The prisoner was under the influence of drink at the time, but she had never seen him before.—Elizabeth HankeV, corroborated the complainant's statement, and stated that she was also kicked about the body by the prisoner for going to the woman's assistance.—Sergeant Chantler said the prisoner was a married man and when charged with tho offence he said he didn't know what he was doing. The magistrates committ(d him to jail for two months.—John Ryan, labourer on the Ship Canal, and lodging at 17, Dial-st., was charged with unlawfully beating and assaulting his wife Mary Ann Ryan, in Bank-st., the previous night. The woman who was al- most unable to walk refused to give evidence against her husband.—Mr. Hunt (Chief Constable) stated that a man named William Donavan heard screams of a woman in Bank-st., and on going in that direr tion he saw the com- plainant down on the ground and the prisoner standing over her. He told the prisoner to let her alone, but he t, Id him to wind his own business. Some lads in the street then commenced to throw stones at the prisoner, and Sergeant Taylor and P.C. Bell heard of the matter and proceeded there. They found the woman lying on the ground unconscious. They took the prisoner to the Police Station, and it was found necessary to take the woman to the Infirmary. The prisoner was charged with the assault and replied "She was stupid, and I just gave her a tip or two with my clogs, just to chastise her." Both the prisoner and his wife had been drink- ing together. Evidence was given in corroboration of the Chief Constable's statement by William Nnavan, David Appleton, Sergeant Taylor, P.C. Bell, and a youth who saw the prisoner kicking the woman.—The magis- trates sent the prisoner to gaol for two months.

A DEAF AND DUMB PRISONER. At the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, John Callon, 10, Hardy-St., and Robert Bsttersby, 10, Hardy- st.. were each charged with being drunk and disorderly on Pinner's Brow, or, Saturday night, and the latter prisoner was also charged with breaking a window in the "Lord Rodney." Battersby, who is deaf and dumb caused great trouble owing to the difficulty in making himself understood. After every other means had been tried to explain to him the nature of the charge against him, Alderman Harrison valourdusly stepped into the breach, and amid much laughter in court made signs to Battersbv to look towards him. He then commenced " talking " to defendant in the deaf and dumb language, the first letter of which consisted in putting his hands into a devotional attitude. The deaf and dumt man however refused to understand. In tbeir dilemma, the magistrates decided to go on with the' case against ' Callon. The evidence showed that he was drunk and very disorderly against the Lord Rodney on Saturday night, as also was Battersby. The latter also smashen 6ne of the windows. The magistrates fined Callon 55., and Battersby was taken into an ante-room where Alderman Harrison went to enlighten him as to the proceedings in the court. After a short time Alderman Harrison returned,and informed the cotirt that Batterslw alleged that he was pushed into Um window, but the witnesses denied this aid the magistrates inflicted a fine ,of I.os. and costs or 1,1

the shop safe on Saturday night, and on Monday morn- ing found it had been broken into,and found three pairs of clogs had been taken. Information was given to the police and D.S. Monaghan made inquiries, and appre- hended the prisoners the previous night. He also suc- ceeded in tracing two pairs of clogs, together with some football clothing which was thought to have been taken from a football club's pavilion at Arpley. The prisoners when charged replied " Yes, we broke into the place about midnight, and sold the clogs." Mr. Spinks applied for a remand until Saturday, which was granted. DRUNK AND DISORDFRLY.—JamPs Foy and James Hayes were fined for this offence in Bank-street, the previous morning, and Daniel Mahoney, was fined ss. , including costs for a similar offence in Church-st, THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes (chairman), Messrs. J. FL Fleming and J. Faircloagh. Datrar.—John Malley was ordered to leave the town for being drunk in Buttermarket-st. the previous after-

noon. A FOOLHARDY SLEEPER-OUT.—G,!.o. Baker was charged with being a rogue and a vagabond found sleeping out in the Bewsey forge, on the previous evening. The night watchman said that he found the prisoner in a very dangerous position in Bewsey forge,as he was lying under the neck end of the furnace, where the red hot slag runs over. If a brick had fallen out, the man would have been burnt to a cinder. Witness had driven him out of the works several times this week.—The magistrates committed him to gaol for seven days. MUSIC LICENSES.—Flerbertl George Galloway applied for a music and dancing license for the Masonic Hall, St. Austin's-lane; John Shaw, applied for a music license for the Strange's Arms public-house, Dial-st. ; and Elizabeth Ann Coop applied for the transfer of the music license of the Hop Pole Inn, from her husband to herself. All the applications were granted. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Alder- man Wright, and Councillor Roberts. DESERTFR.—Wm. Charlton was charged with being a deserter from the First Royal Sussex Regiment, stationed at Portsmouth in December, 1885. He was removed to Strangeways to await an escort. AN OCCASIONAL LICENSE.—MT. Evans, of the Bull's Head, applied for an occasional license to sell at the Gymnasium from 8 o'clock to 2 o'clock last(Friday)night. The application was granted. ASSAULT ON THE FOLlCE.—Martin Casey, of no settled abode, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and with assaulting P.C. Cooper while in the execution of his duty on the previous evening. The officer said the prisoner was coming along Bridge-street on the previous evening in a very drunken state and shouting r that the people of Ireland were better than the people of I England.—Alderman Harrison : "He'd better go there then."—The officer continuing said that he told prisoner Ito go along more quietly, but he commenced insulting witness who was obliged to take him into custody. On the way to the police station, he became very violent, and kicked witness on the hand. He had been very violent on previous occasions when he had been drunk.— The magistrates committed prisoner to gaol for one months' hard lat.our. CRUELTY TO A HORSE.--JOTIRS E itMl and Chas. Eaton, both of Lymm, were summoned ,the former for working a mare while in an unfit state, and the latter for caus- ing it to be so worked on the Bth November. Inspector Luff, R.S.P.C.A., whose first case this was in Warring- ton, stated that on the above date in Bridge-st., he saw the defendant driving a grey mare attached to a cart containing himself and two other persons. The mare was very lame,and had a diseaqed foot. It was in great pain.—P.C. Evans corroborated.—The defendants al- leged that they had received permission from a veterin- ary surgeon to take the horse • out.—Jonas Eaton was fined in the costs 3s. 6c1., and Charles Eaton 103. includ- ing costs.

NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS. SATURDAY.—Before Messrs T. H. Pearson (chairman), J. L. Wood, and R. Stone. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas English, Newton, was fined ss. for committing this offence in Newton on the 3rd inst. THEFT FROM A PAWNSHOP.—James Donohue, a Collier, was charged with stealing from the shop of Wm. Jones, pawnbroker, 27,Market-st., Earlestown, on the 4th inst., a pair of men's trousers, valued Es. 6d.—P.C. Burns stated that he was going along Market-st., on the 4th inst., when he saw the defendant take the trousers and walk off with them. Witness followed and took him into custody.—The magistrates committed him to gaol for 14 days. NIGHT POACHING AT LIAYDOCK.—WM.Ha rri so n,a black- smith, of Haydock, was charged with night poaching at Haydock Park on the 9th inst.—Mr. Stuart, who pro- seeuted, said that he hoped that the magistrates would deal severely with this case. On two or three previous occasions,he had appeared in prosecutions in connection with Haydock Park, and he had then asked for leniency to be extended to the defendants because of the unfor- tunate coal dispute hanging over the district. But their leniency appeared to have been wasted. In the present case the defendant and a number o: other •men were seen at 3.30 a.m. on the 9th inst., by Thomas Martland, the keeper of Haydock Park, busy with nets and also with beating the ground for game. The keeper and his men rushed out at them, and all but he defendant escaped. The other men in their hurry let,. 42 rabbits behind them, which were taken possession of. Priscner was fined 403. and costs, and bound over for three months, himself in £lO, and two sureties of £5. ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A " KNOBSTICK."—Mr. Stuart, solicitor, applied for a warrant against a man whose name he did not know, who assaulted a man named Peter James, at Golborne, at the beginning of last week. The man had met James in a field in Golborne, and knocked him to the ground, injuring him severely, The man then ran off. There was a witness in court who gave a description of the man to P.S. Peters, who was of opinion that he knew the man.—Thomas Unsworth and P.S. Peters each gave evidence, the latter stating that from the description that he had heard, he was satisfied that the man's name was Edward Jones, a sinker at Golborne. The warrant was granted.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Refore Mr. C. Reynolds, Dr. Steele. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY . —Mary Taylor, Rich Brd Tench, Sam Worthington, Alice liampson, Jno. Ryan and James Stewart were each charged with being drunk and disorderly. PITCH AND Toss.—Michael Moores, Thomas Cunniffe, William Lever, Albert Dillon and Joseph Faulkner, boys, were summoned for having on Sunday, the 22nd Octo- ber, played pitch and toss at Belvedere. Faulkner was dismissed and the remainder were each ordered to pay costs 4s. fid. CART WITHOUT NAME. —Ed ward Clarke, farmer, Kingsley, was ordered to pay costs 53. 61, for using a cart without having his name printed thereon. Doo Wrrnour LICENSE .—Jno. Lightfoot, joiner, Preston-o'-th'-Hill, was summoned for keeping a dog without a license.—Dismissed, because ownership not clear. _

THEFT OF Con.—Michael Moores, aged 15, was sum- moned for stealing 21 lbs. of coal, the property of the Manchester Ship Canal Co. He was ordered to pay a fine of ss. or seven da) s hard labour—TWO boys named Herbert G. rye and John Jos. Shaw were each ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod for a similar offence committed that morning. The amount of coal stolen was 30 lbs. FOOTPATH OnsTnucTrox.—Jno. Arthur Clough, a youth, described as a butcher's assistant, was charged With obstructing the footpath in Church-st. Fined 53. KNOCKERS HP AT VARIANCE.—Ann Mary Mercer, young woman of Mill-st., wils summoned for using threats to Thomas Kerfoot, an old man of King-st. Both parties are engaged in the" knocking up " business and it transpired there was some ill-feeling through the com- petition. The case was dismissed. DISCHARGED —Patrick O'Brien, a deaf and dumb man, was charged with stealing a pair of trousers value 6s. and a shirt value Bd., the property of a boatman named Joseph Yates. The prosecutor did not appear and the prisoner was discharged. BEGOING.—Henry Goodwin, a young man, was charged with begging in Church-st., on Satnrday night —The prisoner who pleaded guilty, said he was a glassmaker but was stopped through the coal strike. He was sen- tenced to seven days' hard labour. BAD CHARACTERS.—Mary Murphy, a bad character, was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for being guilty of indecent conduct. For a similar offence Jessie Wood, who had not been before the Court for two years, was fined.lo3. and costs 63. Bd.; and William Lightfoot for aiding and abetting her was mulcted in a similar penalty.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr.G. Comber (chairman), Messrs. John White and James Tinsley. TRESPASSING IN SEARCH OF GAXE.—Richard Reddard and Richard Colley, Sankey Bridges, were charged with haying on the 9th October, at Burtonwood, trespassed on certain land in the possession of Albert Kilshaw, in search of conies. Mr.G. F.F. White prosecuted on behalf of Lord Lilford, :he owner of the estate, who stated that the two defendants were caught on the land by a gamekeeper, with a ferret, rabbit net, and a dog. The same day the defendants had been warned off some other land, and when caught the ferret was in a rabbit bur- row. A gamekeeper in the employ of Lord Lilford said that on the date named he saw the two defendants on Mr.Warburton's field,near a rabbit burrow. He ordercd them away,and at one o'clock he saw them again,wheo they were on Mr. Kilshaw's field. A ferret was in a rabbit hole, and a net was in one of the defendant's pockets, but no game had been caught by them.—The magistrates fined them si.and costs each.

RUPTURE CURED.—S. J. SHERMAN, Hernia Specialist, 64, Chancery-lane London, sends his book on rupture post ree. Branch Chambers. 26, Ring-st., Manche ter. —Advt. Another Peer's son has !joined the ranks of the war correspondents. He is the Hon. Maurice Gifford, the younger brother of Lord Gifford. He is now in Matabeleland, a field to which he was attracted by the South African experiences of his brother. The Hon. Maurice is 34 years old, and he possesses all the Giffords' love of fighting. --- Aye. that is what " flemocea " does. And does it quickly, too—whether it's a toothache or neuralgia with all their shooting pains, or eczema with its painful and distressing irritation—or piles that make thousands of lives wretched. Rheumatism in the joints or muscles has been cured even of years' standing—while for cuts, burns and bruises, its far, very far, ahead of any, oint- ment that has ever been put before the public.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATIIRDAY.—Before Mr. John .Burgess (chairman) and
Mr. L. V,2isey.

DEW IC AND DISORDERLY.—John Davies, a labourer, last from Salop, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in School-street, the previous evening. The prisoner was dismissed on payment of 45. 6d. which amount was found upon the prisoner. MONDAY.—Befnre Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Alderman Harrison, Dr. Gornall, Messrs. W. Pierpoint, T. BirchalLS. Wright and J W. Hayward. FINED FOR DRUNBENNESS.—WiIIiam Lamb, 12 Old- road ; Thomas Bohan, 11 Bank-st. ; Patrick Loughlin, • Locker's-yard; William Benson, 4a Dial-st. ; William Cox' last from Chester; William Hardman, 15 Haydock- Bt. ;Elenry Bell, 39 Frederick-st. PIGEON STEALING —Three boys, Walter Ellis, Brierlev- st., Isaac Lowe, 55 Wakefield-st., and John Whitiaker, 1 Wakefeld-st., were charged with stealing four pigeons ' from John Butcher, 2 Collins-St., on the 10th inst. They were ordered to receive twelve strokes each of the birch , rod. TUESDAL—Before Mr. H. Fleming (chairman), Dr. Starkey Smith and Mr B. Garnett. ANOTHER WIFE ASSALILT.—John Vickers was charged with, beating and assaulting his wife, Ann Vickers, on S tturday night. From the evidence of the complainant, who appeared with two black eyes, it appeared that when the prisoner went home on Sa!urday night he com- menced beating her in the face and caused her to have two black eyes. She stated that her husband had ill- used her ever since she had been married to him.—D.S. Monaghan said the woman had frequently got her face disfigured. The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for two months' hard labour. DETINK.— Catherine Brown, no address, made her 32n i appearance* before the magistrates, charged with being drunk in Smith-sirert, the previous evening. She was sent to prison for 14 days. 1111. RILEY'S CASES.—In the following cases of irregu'ar school attendance, Mr. G. Illey prosecuted. Thomas Bridge, hawker, Winwick-road, 21. 61. ; Charles Camp- bell, railway man, Latchford, 5.. ; Michael Dempsey, tanner, Fennel-stvet, 5. ; Margaret Fallon, lodgjpg- house keeper, Latchford, 2.. 61. ; John Fiddler, spelter porker, Crossley-street, 2. 13.1. ; Jos. WEresrEsnaT.-- -Before Mr. John Geddes (chairman), Alderman Wright, and Mr. J. H. Fleming. - ALLEGED THEFTs.—JoR. Doherty, and James Bartlett, " were charged with breaking in the lork-up shop of John Pirchall, Liverpool-roarl, and stealing thereirom three pairs of clogs, value 81 ad.—lnsoector Spinki said that -complainant John Bircball, ologger, Liverpool-road, left •

RUNCORN V. STOCKPORT " A " TEAMS.—This fixture is one of the most popular matches of the season. Unfor- tunately for Runcorn, they were not able to play their strongest combination, being without the services of Butterworth, full back, and T. Robinson ,at three- . .

qvarter, who were assisting the first team at Stockport. rhe weather was beautifully fine, and there was a fair attendance of spectstors, when the following teams took their positions :—Runcorn : Richardson, full back; Myers, liollingswortn, and W. Gayter, three-quarter hacks; G Robinson and J. Nickson half-hacks; Antro- bus, W. Evans, J. Evans, A. Clarke, Welbe, J. Moores, Shaw, C. Rendlebury, and F. Gayter, forwards. Stock- ' port : Allcock, fullback; Sutcliffe, Burrows, and Faucett, threequarLer backs; Heathcote, Sams, and Lygatt, halt- backs; Goodall, Gibson, Wood, Greenhouse, Mills, Casey, Walker, and Johnson forwards. Burrows started on behalf of the visitors, and a good return was made. After the usual preliminaries the home team quickly at- tacked, and play was located in the Stockport quarters. A forward rush, in which Mills and Goodall were pro- minent, transferred to more neutral ground. From the subsequent pack Robitsson broke away grandly, and threw to Hollingsworth, who passed to Myers, for the latter to make a splendid effort, which was almost suc- cessful. Scrimmaging ensued in close proximity to the visitors' goal, and a _niskick by Allcock almost let in Runcorn, Faucett just averting disaster. Stockport now had a turn of pressing, and aided by some smart loose rushes of their forwards, the home- half was invaded. Here Richardson was put to the test, and proved himself a ,capable custodian. Faulty play by Sams and Faucett, and quick following up by the Runcorn forwards, was the means of bringing relief. Pendlebury being prominent in heading a dribble which caused hostilities to be waged near the visitors' quarter flag. Richardson and Allcock now had a " passage of arms," in which the Buncornian got the best. Stock- port were penalized for off-side play, which again carried the game in more neutral territory. A pretty bout of passing between the home backs was marred by W. Gayter selfishly sticking to the ball, and a glorious open- ing was lost. A minute later Robinson was seen to ad- vantage, for upon getting beautifully away he gave Myres a good pass, and the latter with a brilliant run, beat the opposition, but unfortunately lost the ball. The interval arrived with no advantage to either team. Antrobus started the second moiety, to which Burrows replied, Myers eventually sending to touch near the centre. Stockport had the advantage of the opening, and the home team were forced to defend. W. Evans removed the danger with a fine dribble, Allcock staying his progress. Runcorn now pressed hotly, and the visitors' lines were seriously jeapodized. Nickson and W. Gayter each making good individual efforts to get over. Stockport, aided by strong forward rushes, reached the centre, but their stay was of short duration, as upon Antrobus breaking grandly away from a line out, he passed to Welbe who with no opposition is front mulled the easiest of chances. The end eventually came with neither side having scored any major points. LANCASHIRE CUP COMPETITION. SECOND CLASS. RESULTS UP TO SATURDAY. Pld. Won. Lost. Drn. G. T. G. T. Pts. For. Agst. St. Helens 6 ... 5 ... 1 ... 0 3 9 ... 1 2 ... 10 Ulverston 7 ... 5 ... 2 ... 0 ...13 9 ... 4 1 ... 10 Aspull 7 . 4 ... 2 ... 1 ... 3 4 3 ~, 9 Widnes Leigh 6 .. 4 ... 2 ... 0 ... 7 ... 3 4 ... 6 WalkcL-n 7 . 3 .. 4 ... 0 ... 510 ... 5 1 ... 6 Lancaster 7 ... 3 ... 4 ... 0 ... 5 6 ... 6 5 ... 6 R'daleSt.Ci'ts7 ... 2 ... 3 ... 2 ... 3 4 ... 7 4 ... 8 liloss'ev 7 . 1 . 4 ... 2 ... 3 2 ... 613 ... 4 Bl‘ckleti 7 0 7 ~, 0 1 0 —ll 18 ... 0 WIDNES V. LEIGIL—Tha above teams faced each other OU Saturday, on the Widnes ground, before about 2,000 spectators. Drummond, county half-back, was enthus- iastically cheered when he stepped on the field. Barber started the game, and the visitors at once attacked, and kept the home men on the defensive. Ten minutes after the game had bees in progress, Anderton scored for Leigh, and Ewan kicked an easy goal. The visitors still pressed heavily, and were almost over again, but Brennan nicely saved. The Widnesians pulled together finely after this, and made their way down the field. Barber got possession, and put in a splendid run, but was floored. Toohey then get the leather, and passed to Clarke, who landed home amid tremendous cheers. Drummond made a fine attempt at goal, but the ball I struck the post. This was decidedly hard lines. The 1 success seemed to infuse life into the home men, who worked up well, but the visitors gradually got down the field. Smart play, in wheels Alford° was conspicuous, trrnsferred the game once more in a favourable position for the home team, but the determined defence of the opponents prevented. At half-time the score stood Leigh 1 goal, Widnes I try. On resumption of play, Brennan played as a three-quarter man, and Tooliey went full back, where he proved very useful. The homesters at once put on pressure. Alter play had been resumed about five minutes a penalty kick was allowed the chemicals, from which Barber landed a splendid goal. Leigh dribbled down the ground and made matters look rather dangerous, but a long kick by Drummond sent the ball in touch, near the home goal line, where several exciting scrimmages took place. Leigh at length got the ball free and rushed down field, Toohey making a splendid save. The oval was returned to mid-field. when Barber had to be taken off the field injured. De- spite the fact of being a man short, the home team severely pressed their opponents. Gordon got possession and reached home safely amidst cheers, but the kick was futile. The remainder of the game was played in Isemidarkness. The result was a good victory for Wid- nes, by nine points to five. RUNCORN Ho RIVETS V. RUNCORN VICTORIA.—These keen rivals met on the ground of the former. Th. Hor- nets were without J. Billington, half back, and T. Sut- ton, three-quarter, who were replaced by J. Brown and S. Wcrthington. The Victories won the toss and played up hill. Percival started the ball, which was well re- turned by Johnson. Soon after Jolley scored a splendid try for the Hornets, the goal kick failing. This seemed to rouse the Vies a little, but the strong defensive game of the Hornets held them at bay. Jolley scored again for the Hornets, Hignett kicking a fine goal. On the change of ends the Hornets had all the best of the play, the forwards playing a gra, d game. Jolley scored again, Hignett kicking a goal. Cm:flip added another try, and time was called with the scdre :—Hornets,two geals,two trys, eight minors ; Victories, nothing. WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND V. BRINNINGTON 2ND. These teams met at Stockport, the homesters started the game, the opening stages found the visitors pressing and ultimately by smart play Brobbin scored an un- improved try. The home team retaliated and took play down the field, where Lawson drooped a clever goal, which proved to be the winning point, the Rang- ers retiring defeated by four points to three. RUNCORN VICTORIA A V. WIDNES HORNETS.—PIayed at Runcorn, on Saturday. The Hornets won the toss and kicked off, Ratsliffe returning, after good play on both sides half time ending in no score. Victoria restartet the game, and Spencer getting possession scored a grand try, Shingler making a good attempt at gee!. Spencer scored a second try from a pass by Mills. The final re suit was—Runcorn Victoria, two tries ; Widnes Hornets, nil. WARRINGTON RANGERS V. BRINNINGTON (STOCKPORT). —Played at Lovely-lane, on Saturday last, when the home team held the upper hand throughout and finally won by 3 tries to nil. P.

ASSOCI AT lON . WARRINGTON Ir. MANCHESTER WANDERERS.—This match was played.on Saturday last on the Northern Lawn Tennis Ground at Old Trafford. Warrington were minus Mather, Linaker,and Connor whilethe Wanderers had two silo' t and decided to play with nine men. The visitors kicked off and at once rushed down the field, but Orford relieved. The home side next became prom- inent by a good run on the right wing, but their efforts were fruitless. Some good passing by the Warrington forwards resulting in Denby scoring the first goal. After the kick off Fennellv got the ball at his feet,rushed down the field and scored with a beauty. The game was very even up to half-time, Clarke at full back was doing good work. flail-time score, Warrington 2, Wan- derers nil. The second half opened tamely,the Warring- ton full backs having little difficulty in clearing against three forwards. The Wanderers scored a goal from a free kick just in front and Norman scored a third goal I for Warrington. Even play followed and when the whistle blew Warrington won a most enjoyable game by three goals to one. FRIENDS SCHOOL, FENEETH. v. FARNwORTH.—This match was played at FRI rirOrth Penketh having won the toss played up hill. The Farnworth forwards at once attacked, and in five minutes scored two goals. Thence until half-time the score remained the same. After the re-start, from a foul in the goal mouth, Nicholson put the ball through, and made the score 2-1. Good work was done by the Penketh forwards, but the opposing halves and backs playing the man, no othel• goal resulted until neirly time, when one of the Farnworth backs put the ball thringh his own goal. Meanwhile the forwards had scored three times, so the game ended—Farnworth 5 • Friends' School, 2. PENAETH VILLACIE v. 'BROADHEATIL—On Saturday the above teams met on the Recreation Grounds, Pen- keth, when, after a well-contested game, victory rested with the Penkethites by five goals to nil.
