div.p: RUGBY.
WARRINGTON v.. BARROW:

A good t;;,;;;b-W.OF spectators assembled on the Causeway field on Saturday. to witness the match between Barrow and the home team, in their trial of strength in the cup competition. The visitors occupy a very modest place in the statistical calender of the corn petition—indeed they have the distinction of being on the bottom rung but one. Nevertheless, the game waA a very enjoyable one throughout. Boscow, who is still resting had his position filled by Heesom,and in addition to this, Nevins was absent. Immediately after Turner started, the Warrington forces invaded the domains of their opponents with an amount of dash and individual effort, which caused the men from Barrow to become both apprehensive and very alert. Presently Dickenson of the Barrow threequarters made a dexterous pass along his line, with the result that the leather was sent by a kick from Baker, into midfield. But it slid not remain here long. A forward rush, fed from threequarters,soon brought the oval within a few feet of the goal line. And then commenced a struggle which continued for some ten minutes, the visitors fighting with the obstinacy of despair against the skillfully combined efforts of the two Bates, assisted by the threequarter backs. At length by a wily run Marshall galloped into midfield with the ball thus averting the immediate danger. From here Carey getting p i:s3ssion made a drop at goal, but the ball landed near the feet of Barrow full back, who mulled, and only just piloted the leather from near the line, by a series of frantic kicks. Later, Dickenson, collared the ball and made a dash towards the Warrington line, but was quickly overhauled by Webster, and after which fine exchanges between Heesom, Bell, and Chapman, enabled Carey to obtain a free kick. While the kick at goal was being taken the Barrow men unburdened them- selves of their celebrated warhoop, which they repeated afterwards on the occasion of other free kicks. Another piece of give and take play followed, followed by a free kick by "Fair " Turner, brought play once more on to the verge of the visitors' line. For a:time the play was simply fast and brilliant the visitors defending for all , they knew, while Warrington, skillful and dogged, were repelled not an inch from the vantage point they had gained. Presently, with an almost increditable alertness J. Bate picked up from a scrimmage, passed to his agile namesake, who with scarcely more than one bound, found himself over the goal line, a performance which was greeted with quite a tumult of applause. Heesom failed to augment. No more scoring was done this half but after therestart,the Barrow men forced play over half line, and an attempt to reach the line, initiated by some splendid three-quarter play, was "nipped in the bud" by an able defence by Webster. The Northerners were again repelled and driven near to their line, when, after a scrimmage, Jolley outshone himself by the bril- liancy of a try which he succeeded in notching. Turner failed at the kick. Foot play ensued for a time. Pre- sently Taylor charged a kick of Dickenson's, and a score seemed imminent, when Bowker, fielding finely, punted out of danger. John Bate appealed for a try a few minutes later, but was over-ruled,and next Sharp inter- cepted a pass, and racing away with a clear field he eventually passed to Dickenson. The latter was running strongly until Webster appeared on the scene, but fortu- nately for Barrow the line was reached, and the effort culminated in Sharp scoring at the corner, the same player failing at goal. A long run by Turner should certainly have been turned to good account, but a wild , pass gave Barrow another chance,which was fortunately nipped in the bud by Evans. Prolonged struggles ensued on the Barrow line,and finally Bowker saved. The War- ringtonians did not relax their energies, and the visitors were from now to the call of time forced to defend, and though James and John Bate, Evans, and Potts were all within an ace of scoring, there was no addition, and the final result read :—Warrington, two tries (six points) Barrow, one try (threc points). Teams :—Warrington : F. fleesom, back ; C. Potts, Carey, J.W.Evans, and H.Webster,three-quarter backs ; James Bate and John Bate, half-backs; Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, J. T. Phillips, T. Donohue, J. Taylor, 4. Berry, E. Bailey, and J. T. Thorniley, forwards. Barrbw : Wood- house, back; Bel, Dickenson, Baker, and T. Bowker, three-quarter backs; Marshall and Chapman,half backs; J. Bowker, Satterthwaite, Carter, Sharp, Parkinson, Gormley. Greaves, and M'Donald, forwards.

RUNCORN v. STOCKPORT.—A great amount of interest was taken at Stockport in the match with Runcorn, on Saturday. Considerable feeling is felt in the hatters' town at the inclusion of so many Runcorn men in the Cheshire county team, and great preparations had been made to give the Runcorn team a warm reception and a good licking. Much disappointment was felt that Houghton and Saville were both on the injured list, and could not assist their respective sides. For Runcorn Butterworth, from the "A "team, took Houghton's place,and Halsnead took Saville's place on the Stockport side. The teams were :—Runcorn: J. Butterworth, back ; 'l. Robinson, T. Warder, W. Faulkner, and E. F. Morris, three-quarter backs; S. Abrams, and J. Faulk- ner, half backs; J. Langley, R. Reece, H. Farmer, J. Davies, A. Taylor, J. Stubbs, H. Williams' and W. Light- foot, forwards. Stockport: J. T. flaslam, back; J. Ashton, S. Bailey, J. Halsnead, and another, three- quarter backs; J. Pickard and G. Norris, half backs ; Dr. Smith, J. Spect, J. Potts, W. Bailey, T. King, J. Mottershead, J. Beard, and Murray, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. H. Payne, Lancashire county. Faulkner started against the wind, and Stockport, by the aid of Bailey, pressed the Runcorn backs, and Morris having his kick charged, the home side were nearly in. Butterworth kicked in touch near the line. The throw. out ended in a scrimmage near the Runcorn line, and for a considet- able time Stockport tried the defence very much. Morris got the ball away, only to see a forward rush get up again into close quarters, and during some passing, Faulkner was held under the Runcorn posts, a penalty kick being awarded for not playing the ball. Hasiam made a miserable attempt atan easy place. Succeeding the drop-out, play continued central, when a rush by Speet and King took the ball to the Runcorn end, and during a run along the touch-line Halsnead went in touch when clear of all opposition. The following play was of a very close nature, chiefly forward. What little pass- ing was done was on the Runcorn side, and at half-time nothing had been scored. After the interval matters somewhat changed. When Warder hrl returned, the ball was kept well in the home half, where Runcorn experi- enced very hard luck in not scoring several times. Butterworth' who had played a champion game through- out, got the ball in his own half, and stoadied himself for a drop at goal, the ball going over the bar. This was a very fine piece of play. It was not long before Abrams throw to Warder, who outwitted his opponents and got over the line, the goal-kickiag failing. The advantage thua gained was now kept, and Stockport was penned in their side of the half-way line, and were very lucky to come off so lightly. The final result was —Runcorn, one dropped goal, one try ; Stockport, nothing.
DESPERATE STRUGGLE WITH THIEVES AT ST. HELENS. --- A POLICE CONSTABLE KILLED.

THREE ARRESTS. About eleven o'clock on Sunday night Constables cordon and Whalley were on duty in Pocket Nook, St. Helens, when they were informe4 that some men had entered the engineering works of Mr. John Fa,rster. The officers went to the place, and there saw that a hencote had been broken open and three men were in a corner prepared to defend themselves against arrest. As soon as the officers appeared the men threw stones, slag, and every other available missil3, and the offcers, before they could close with the men, were badly injured. The struggle, which was very severe, lasted for sometime, and in the end, a man named John Carney, of Smithy Brow, was arrested and taken to the Town Hall. Later on another man' John Leahy, of Smithy Brow, was arrested by Whalley. The other man, Frank Riley, was arrested at a quarter to eleven on Monday morning. Gordon was badly cut on the face and had two serious wounds on both sides of the head. About three o'clock on Monday morning he went to the surgery of Dr. M'Nicoll, police surgeon, where Dr. Jameson dressed the wound and ordered him home to bed. He went to his lodgings, 178, Westfield-street and got to bed, but at seven o'clock when a man who slept in the same room _ . .

awoke he found that Gordon was dead. Further inquiries show that Gordon was struck on the head with a bar of iron,but when he went to the doctor's he did not appear to be seriously injured, and remained on duty a short time afterwards. When he went to bed tie told young Pratt, son of the laudlofd, about the occurrence, and Pratt asked him if he would have any- thing to drink before he went to sleep. He said " No." When Pratt awoke he looked at Gordon, and found him dead. He had breathed rather heavily, but Pratt did not stsspect anything serious. Constable Whalley was struck and kicked, but his injuries were only slight. The scene of the struggle was visited by a large num- ber of persons on Monday. The hencote is about five yards long and of corresponding height. It is con- structed of wood. There is a window, which is barred inside, and when a pane was broken and the men found themselves confronted by iron bars, they smashed off the padlock with a large furnace rake. The yard is en- closed by a wall nine feet high, and loose slag and stone are laid on the ground for paving. Three colliers, named James Carney, John Leahy, and Frank Riley, were brought before Alderman Cook and M'Kechnie, Councillor J. B. Leach and Mr. D. Chad- wick, at St. Helens, on Wednesday morning. Chief Constable Wood said the men were only charged that day with having broken and entered a hencote at the Atlas Works of Councillor John Forster, and stolen therefrom some poultry, value 7s. 6J. About eleven o'clock on Sunday night Constables Whalley and Gordon were on duty near the works, and from what they were told they entered by means of a key which Whalley had been supplied with. On getting inside they found the window of the hencote had been broken ; the padlock had also been broken and the door was open. On look- inside they saw the prisoner Carney and Riley, and the officers Went into them. Carney knocked the lamp out of the constable's hand, and Riley atruels CtOrdQui face. Gordon seized hold of Riley and Whalley seized Carney and dragged him out of the cote. Leahy then struck Whalley a severe blow on the back of the head with a brick. Carney ran away. Leahy afterwards came up and struck Gordon a violent blow with a bar of iron on the head. All three prisoners, who were then in the yard, commenced to throw stones and bricks at the constables. Whalley then knocked Carney down, and a violent struggle ensued, in. which Gordon was violently kicked and struck. Carney was taken into M`Bricle'a works, and afterwards removed to the Town Hall. Three-quarters of an hour later Leahy wz ar- rested at his own house, and Riley was arrested that morning just before the court commenced its sitting. He (the Chief Constable) intended to offer sufficient evidence to justify a remand until Thursday. Police Constable Whalley, who had been injured in the back in the struggle, said when he and Gordon went into the cote he saw Riley and Carney. (At this point all the prisoners declared that Riley was not there.) Whalley put the lamp in Carney's face, and he knocked it out of his hand. They all struggled to the door and got out- side. Witness was struck by Leahy in the back with a brick. Oa going towards the yard gate Gordon was hit on the aide of the head with a bar of iron. Riley got away, and all three went up the yard and commenced to throw missiles. Leahy went up a spout and dropped in Barber-st. The other two went through the wicket gate into Atlas-st. The officers followed and knocked Carney. down and arrested him. Riley got away, but Leahy was arrested three-quarters of an hcur afterwards. When charged Leahy replied, "1 am not guilty. I had nothing to do with it." Cainey said, " I never stole them, and know nothing about them." The three fowls had been killed and their heads pulled off. Riley repeated that he was not there.—Prisoners were then remanded until Thursday.—Carney said: We should like to go to Liverpool, and stop there, and not stop here.—Chief Constable Wood : But I want you to stop here for the present. THE INQUEST.—VERDICT OF WILFUL MURDER. Mr. Samuel Brighouse, the county coroner, opened the inquest on the deceased constable in the Police Court, Town Hall, on Thursday. The greatest interest was manifested in the case. The court was crowded and many were unable to gain admission. Additional ac- commodation was provided for the reporters in the space behind the jury. A special jury of fifteen gentlemen had been empanelled so that in case two or three might not coincide with the views of the general body there would be a margin to allow of a verdict from the neces- sary "twelve good men and true." Mr. G. J. G. Critchley was selected as foreman, the other jurors be- ing Messrs. J. EL Houghton, E. S. Ilenty, J. B. Warren, W. Greenwood, James Latham, W. Fletcher, J. Hulme, E. Abel. Robert Coop, J. Farrell, W. Gerrard, J. P. Morris, T. Baxter and, J. Iloulton.—The jury accom- panied by the coroner, viewed the body, and subse- quently visited the scene of the outrage. The three prisoners were placed in the dock during the inquiry.— Mr. W. 3. Jeaves, town clerk, appeared on behalf of the police, Chief Constable Wood also being present. Mr. H. L. Riley watched the case on behalf of Lcahey and Riley the other prisoner being unrepresented.—Constahle Whalley next gave evidence in which the detailed cir- cumstances of the struggle. In reply to Mr. Riley he said they had only the light for a brief space at the hen- cote. The whole of the three prisoners had thrown stones. Mr. Riley submitted that the men were only responsible for their individual acts of violence. Although the prisoners might have set out with the common object of robbing a hen roost, still one might be perfectly willing to submit to arrest while another might defy it. The Coroner said all the three had thrown stones together, and were all responsible for the acts. Caruey then asked a number of questions, alleging that when Whalley struck at him with his staff he missed him, and hit his fellow officer, who shouted out, " Oh, John, you have struck me." Whalley, he said, struck him twice, but tte third time he missed him, and hit Gordon, and it was that which caused the bleeding. At the conclusion of Constable Whalley's evidence the prisoner Carney said that the police had dragged him all the way from Atlas- st., to M`Bride's works, and that when they got him into the police office they kicked him for half an hour. Constable Hall said he saw Carney and Gordon at ftl•Bryde's Works, Carney said, "I have been led into this this time ; it is the first time I ever assaulted a ' policeman." Deceased said, " Well, you have assaulted me now ; have you not ?" " Well," replied Carney, "I am not the only one." Gordon said, " Who are thelwo other men ? " Prisoner replied, "I don't know them, but I wish 1 was at work again. Inspector Goodall said be also saw Gordon at Arßryde's on Sunday at midnight and described his injuries. After Gordon had finished his statement Carney said, " Yts, you--if you had only been by yourself I would have done for you. I will yet, and I will do for Whalley as well. Li-ahoy was brought into the office immediately after Gordon had finished his statement„ and pointing to Leahey Go dun said," That's the man that struck rne with the iron bar." In reply to Mr. Riley, the iespa tor said nCt bar of iron had been found at Forster's works with hair on. it. Mr. Riley questioned whether Carney's clogs had irons on them. One of Carney's clogs was then taken. off, and was found to have irons upon it. Prisoner admitted they were the same clogs that he wore on Sunday night. Medical evidence was next called. Dr. M'Nicoll, police-surgeon and medical officer of health, said he saw Gordon about two o'clock on Monday morning last at his surgery. A post-mortem examination had been made. The deceased was a fine specimen oE a well de- veloped man. There were only two wounds visible out- wardly. No natural cause for eeAth could be found. Deceased died from the blows, which produced shock or concussion. In his opinion deceased had died from failure of the heart, brought about by shock to the ner- vous system, caused by blows.—Dr. Frederick John Knowles, who had assisted in the post mortem, added that there was also a slight cut on the little finger of the left hand. He attributed death to failure ot the heart,. due to shock to the nervous system brought about by violence. The Coroner summed up, and said if three person went with a criminal intent to do a criminal act, and only one of them did the act, while the other two looked on and assented, all three were equally liable and res- ponsible for the consegi trees. The medical evidence was conclusive that death was due to violence. The jury retired at seven minutes past four, and dur- ing the interval of waiting Leahey's mother and Riley's wife sobbed bitterly. They got to the side of the dock to talk to the prisoner's, but were put back by the con- stables. Mrs. Li-ahoy continued in great distress, and wailed " Oh, my child, what did you go with them for." After an absence of five minutes the jury returned with a verdict of wilful murder. FUNERAL OF THE VICTIM.

The funeral cif the police-const.ble on Thersday alter- no ,n excited all extraordinary am,- unt of interest in the town, the body being conveyed to toe cemetery to the music of the Sc. Helens Engineers' Rand and accoro- partied by all the borough police-efliters off duty, with Chief-ronstable Wood and Inspectors Steele and tioodall and thirty Qt the Liverpool conatabutary at present in

the borough, with Inspector Jackson. The body was brought from the constable's late lodgings in Westfield- et. to the Town-hall, from whence the procession took place to the cemetery. The Rev. J. Brown, Presbyterian minister, read the funeral service. The coffin bore the inscription, "James Gordon, aged 26 years, died Nov. 13th." Wreaths were sent by the members of the Pres- byterian Young Men's Association, from the borough police, and from the Liverpool officers.

div.head: DECEASED CONSTABLE.
div.p: THE DECEASED CONSTABLE.

James Gordon was a native of Kincardineshire, and there worked as a farm servant. He came direct to St. Helens five years ago, and then joined the borough police force. He was a single man, and twenty seven years of age. He has a brother, Robert Gordon, in the Lanca- cashire County Force, who was prior to the strike sta- tioned near Manchester. At the commencement of the strike he was dratted to the colliery district of Leigh, and has remained there since. Revisited t. Helens on Monday, having been apprised of his brother's. death by the St. Helens police. The keenest regret is felt by all members of the St. Helens police force at the death of young Gordon, who was held in high esteem by all ranks. The Coroner (Mr. S. Brighouse), ordered a post- mortem examination to be made, and this was done by Dr. M'Nicoll (police surgeon) and Dr. Fred Knowles.

div.head: ANOTHER GREAT FIRE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ANOTHER GREAT FIRE AT ST. HELENS.
COLLAPSE OF THE STEAM FIRE-ENGINE. FAILURE OF WATER SUPPLY.

About half-past nine o'clock on Monday night, information was received at the St. Helens Town Hall that afire was raging at the Greenbank works of the United Alkali Company, and Superintendent Rutherford, with the Steam fire-engine and other appliances, was soon out. The superintendent was driving the steamer, with six members of the brigade on the box, down Hardshaw-street at a 'great rate. He took the left side of the road, so as to get a clear sweep to the right into Church-street, when the hind wheel caught the kerbstone so violently that it was broken off at the axle, and the whole of the occupants were thrown off. A scene of great confusion ensued. The horses were prancing wildly about, and the firemen were struggling to their feet. A crowd of people collected, and as much assistance was .rendered as was possible. A fireman named John Seddon, who lives in Bryon-street, and is employed in the water department of the Corporation, appeared to be badly injured, and he was carried into the Fleece Hotel. police-constable Evans took charge of the unfortunate man, and as he was unable to proceed home, the police ambulance was telephoned for. Dr. Masson called, and found that Seddon was suffering from severe shock,with bruises on the thigh and lett side, but he was unable to say on Monday night whether there were any fractures. While this was going on the horses were got from the disabled engine and run hack again to the Town Hall for the manual. They came galloping down Hardshaw-straet on their second journey, and on the same turn caught the steam fire-engine, which , had not been moved. They, however, continued ; their course, and on arriving at the works found th9.,t the: canal, whlcli 15 the We? water gupply in the neighbour- -a_ h toOd, h been run off, and there was nothing but mud in the channel. This series of unfortunate circumstances appeared to render the presence of the brigade useless, and policemen and firemen were nonplussed how to pro- ceed. The fire during this time was blazing furiously among the vitrol chambers, which are on an elevation of chemical waste seventy or eighty feet high. It will be remembered that early in this year, during a great gale, the Greenbank chimney, which towered to a height of 250 feet was blown down, and in its fall destroyed a large quantity of valuable property below. The chimney was rebuilt, and the structures which were blazing were in close proximity to the great chimney in question, and had been rebuilt or repaired as it was found necessary. There were four vitriol chambers, each, with the con- tents, said to be worth £l,OOO. They each consist of a brick building, on the top of which a huge lead cistern is fixed. The cistern in its turn is covered by a wooden shed, so that the whole forms a structure of great height. The fire had evidently started in No. 4 chamber, the timber of which was speedily demolished, and the lead- work began to melt. The flames then caught the next chamber, and at eleven o'clock that was nearly de- molished. The vitriol from the chamber was running away in a stream to Garden-strmet, where it lay several inches deep. The wind was blowing over the other wooden structures, and what efforts the firemen could make at that hour were being directed to saving the other chambers. Cottage property in the street below the blazing sheds were in considerable danger. Crowds of people were flocking to the place at a late hour, the flames having been seen for a lone distance round. The fire was got under about four o'clock on Tuesday morning, but the firemen remained several hours after- wards. Three vitriol chambers were destroyed. The damage is roughly estimated at £5,000, and the pro- perty is insured in the National Assurance Company of -reland and several other companies.

div.p: letter% to tin Odor.

THE NEW ALDERMAN.—A MISSING 'SPEECH. Sir,—l scanned your paper last week to see the report of the new (publican's) alderman's speech, on WA elec- tion, but in vain. Will you kindly tell me—first wheth.r he returned thanks ; and, secondly, if not, why not? And oblige yours One of the MANY desirous of KNOWING.

TUE TEETOTALERS. Sir,—There seems to me to be a great many hard words said lately about the Conservative publicans that have been returned as representatives in our Town Council. Now as an ardent Liberal, I must protest against the bigoted teetotal party on our side. As one that has lived in Bewsey for a number of years, (and this is without doubt a Liberal ward) I emphatically say, that this bigoted teetotalism is injuring our cause more than a great many are aware of. No doubt teetotalism is an grand thing in its own way, but perhaps modera- tion is quite as good ; but why mix the thing up with politics? I firmly believe that had not Dr. flxiston stated at the first onset that he should support Sunday closing, h.e.would have been a lot nearer the mark. In conclusion I may say that in my opinion there is no one more bigoted than Tories and teetotalers.—Youra res- pectfully,

div.head: CATHERINE-STREET.
div.p: CATHERINE-STREET.
COUNCILLOR ROBERTS' PROTEST.

Sir,—l want to express in your columns_the sense of ndebtedness which I, along with many others, feel to Mr. Councillor Roberts for his vigorous protest agairst the election of Mr. Ashton as Alderman of this Borough. He may or may not have been wise in the strong step he took in " defying" the ruling of the Mayor, but that he was justified in protesting against the arbritary pro- ceedure decided on in this instance I feel no doubt what- ever. A more high-handed and tyrannical course it is impossible to conceive, and all the more so because it was, as I believe, unprecedented. The Town Clerk's ruling, I venture to consider, had no true justification, and as has already been pointed out, it was a departure from previous precedent. notice that in other towns discussion frequently takes place as to the merits of persons proposed for their municipil honours, and rightly so, if such discussion avoids offensive personali- ties. I wish Mr. Councillor RobeAs to feel that in this matter he has the good opinion of a large number of people in this town who are ashamed that the Town Council showers its honours upon members of a trade which has done so much to dishonour the town. I hope better days will come, and trust that all who really care for the elevation of our borough will use every proper endeavour in the future to secure the presence at its j Council Chamber of the best men of all sects and peril ties.—Yours faithfully, JOHN YONGE.

My" efforts "says this " garbler of facts " have been directed, like those of ‘• Cymro "todo my b"st . . . to stay the merciful hand of charity, or brotherly love, and help by slander- ing the colliers and their leaders," &c:, icc. As to the "staying." &c., charity begins at home ; the innocent victims of this unhappy dispute have first claim upon us. As to the " slander "—will Mr. Brouchemite kindly point to anything I have said warranting so harsh a term? I have objected to intimidation ; believiag that every man has the right to carry his labour to the best market and to sell it at the best price he can obtain. Our Eng- lish law professes to secure this right to one and all. Does Mr.Brouchemite uphold the practice of cracking the skulls of those men who have so exercised their un- doubted right to do work interdicted by the federation? If it be Mr.B.'s idea of slander to say that Mr. S. Wcods, M.P., ought, by word and deed, to do his best to prevent , this breach of English privilege, I here emphatically I repeat it. The Federation, so applied, is, in my opinion, a form of conspiracy against the liberty of the subject. This is the sum of my contention; perhaps Mr. Brom- Idemite will now kindly show where the " slander " comes in ? I have dealt with him alone of the two who favoured you last week on this topic, because he alone had the honesty to back his opinions with his name. As to the frothy aeionymity who prostitutes the sacred ' name of " Common Justice" by using it as a cowardly concealment for a cowardly attack, lain content to leave him to the appreciation of Mr. Brouchemite's " intelli- gent readers. Tne man confesses himself to he " half mad " and in his ravings fully substantiates the asser- tion; he demands only our pity and forbearance. What be thought of a man who would hail with any kind? div.head: JOHN PEERS.
div.p: JOHN PEERS.
lIONIE RULE AND TFI PA PROTESTANT MINORITY.

Sir.—Mr. J. C. Dalton in yours of Saturday last,again attempts to throw his Popish dust into our eyes. He would have us think his history true. He charges me with making haphazard statements. This is not true. The massacre of St. Bartholomew in France in 1572 is a fact of history ; the then Pope had the "Te Deum" chanted in Rome to return thanks for the extirpation of the heretics; he also ordered a medal to be struck off, a copy of which I possess, and there is an oil painting in the Vatican in which the murder of Coligny is the sub- lent. istr__D. says I am an "Orange fanatic " and a "belli- cose Orangeman." This is another untruth, for I never was an Orangeman. He places before your readers Cardinal Alarming. Well, I must tell Mr. D., as I once told a Popish priest, "that when Manning joined the church he sold his reason." Listen, Mr. D., to what your grand advocate for Home Rule wrote on the sys- tem of Popery, and bear in mind it is the system I con- tend against, and not individuals.- W. E. Giadstme, M.P., in h s " Vatican Decrees," p. 6, says, "Rome has Substitaed for the proud boast of semper radom a policy of violence and change of faith. Tha.t no one can now become her convert without renouncing his moral and mental freedom, and placing his civil loyalty and duty at the mercy of another." and in his (W. E. G.'s) " Vaticanism " he writes : "I have stated that the Pope condemns liberty of the Press and liberty of speech. His (the Pope's) condemnation is illustrated by his own practice as Governor in the Roman States, where no opinion could be spoken or printed but such as he ap- proved. It is not possible, in the limited space here at my command, adequately to exhibit a strte of facts, thus created by the highest authorities of the Roman Church which I shall not now shrink from calling hor- rible and revolting in itself,and dangerous to the morals of society, the etructure of the family, and the peace of life," p.p. 21,22, 27, published be John Murray,London, 1875. Mr. D., are these haphazard statements ? Weil, sir,Cardinal Wiseman affirmed on oath : "Heretics,schi- maticS, and rebels to our Lord the Pope or his foresaid successors I will to zny utmost power persecute and wage war with "—see correspondence published in the "Times," November, 1850, and in pamphlets, copies in any possession. Canon Stowell,of Manchester, preached a sermon, subject : " One Lord, one faith, one baptism," result, he drove Wiseman out of Manchester for ten years. Popery cannot stand the test of the Scriptures, for the modern creed is not in it. Wiseman and Manning put their imprimatur to the "Glories of Mary," a book full of the grossest absurdities ever printed. Professor Gilmartin, of Maynooth College, last year published a manual of Church history (i e., Papal history), and Archbishop Walsh gave it his Imprimatur. In p. 226 he says: " Universal religious tolerance is as indefensive in theory, as it has been found impossible in practice. And the more one loves religious truth (!),and the spiritual interests of his neighbour, the more must we seek, within the limits of justice and prudence, to etamp out heterdoxy." Does this look like tolerance? Until Mr. D. gives proofs of the grave charge of inhu- manity of the late Dean bleNeile, I shall put it down as another untruth.—Yours truly, ROBERT FOULKES. Frodshana, November 14th, 1893.

_ bir,—ln your last issue, there appeared a letter from Mr. Brouchemite, of the Cosmopolitan Hotel. Friars- green, in which he credits me with being either" A Waster's friend, an agent, or probably a master " mean- ing a colliery proprietor, of course. I can assure him, and your reiders generally, that I am neither ; at the same time I disclaim being an enemy to any man—much less to a collier—and I believe I am m_oro a collier's friend when I wish him to do his part to bring this dispute to an end, by accepting arbitration or by any other mode that may do so, than Ildr.Brouchemite who, by denounc- ing the masters in languige alike unjustifiable and incor- rect and by firebrand denouncement does his utmost to prolong the strife. He might just as well call me a railway director as either of the above. I am simply an old workingman, having lived and worked among celliers all my life, my wife a collier's daughter, and neice and • cousin to a lot or colliers living in mutual respect with them all. Is it likely dud I can be otherwise than friendly with the colliers as a body. At the same time, I abhor a strike, knowing how they generally terminate. it case in pornt is the cotton strike not twelve months since ? Who got anything out of that ? Certainly not the cotton operatives,for to my per- sonal knowl-dge they were heavy losers. I ds know, -sir, what I am talking or rather writing about—it is no

secret in Oldham that steam coal is delivered there from Swansea at Us. a ton : ss. for coal and 6s. for freight, , which is I think, reasonable, for conveying a ton weight 1200 miles, for say, three eighths of a penny per ton ler mile. If agricultural produce, fish, and food generally were conveyed at that rate we should not have much to complain ef. Ido not know yet—neither does anyone al. —that the Government have a legal right to the tames. They may haves moral right, but the legal r. 4111, nos )e. to be tought for and won, and the battle will be a fierce one and long contested. Mr. Brouchemite accuses me of slandering the miners, This I deny. I have donounced outrage,intimidation, the wrecking of homes, the blowing up of houses, and inCendiarism generally—these are incidents of the strike and will be condemned by all right thinking p, ople. Are the colliers the only people who require charity ? What about the victims of this strike who are idle for the want of coal. There are thousands starying to-day for wham Alfred Broththeinite and "Common Justice" seem to have no sympathy left—it is all f)r the colliers. "Common Justice "in your columns says the colliers are fighting his battle and the battle of every working- man in the kingdom." They are fighting mine with a vengeance. They have made me £2O the poorer up to now and ruined many a hundred homes. Every town and village in five or six counties is the worse for the strike—families impoverished, furniture and clothing gone, nothing left but bare walls and empty clothes chests—and where is the compensation to come from when the battle is over and the victory won ? It is not won yet. I wish it was, and that the miners were going in to-morrow at an advance instead of a reduction. Mr. B. and " Commoo Justice" rave and spout of " might and right," !' humanity," benevolence," "brotherly love," " charity," &c., with all such nauseating humbug. Bah ! It is sickening. They des- cribe the colliery owner as a tyrant, a liar and a robber, who would rob the p or man and his family of their rights. The masters declare, and offer to prove,that they cannot pay the late rate of wages with coal at late rates and they offer inspection of their books in proof. "But," say certain gentlemen, "do not believe them, they are making immense profits and can pay." Now, I would ask a plain simple question Is it likely that these men would stop their pits at great cost simply to starve the colliers and their families and burst up the federation? Common sense says no. They, like other business men, study their own interests better, and are not likely to cut off the nose to spite the face. A little concession and forbearance in July could have prevented this disastrous strike with all its irritating effects, and every one would have been the better and there need have been no beg- gary, desolation and misery, such as we now see and ~ear so much of and which so many of us feel so acutely. —I am, sir, yours respectfully, .....
CYMRO.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, MAGAZINES, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, MAGAZINES, &c.

-- A new edition oft' Jerusalem the Holy City ; its His- tory and Hope" by Mrs. Oliphant, was issued in Oct. from the press of Messrs. Macmillan and Co., (price 103. 81.) The illustrations are from wood engravings by Hamilton Aida, and photographs by F. M. Good. To those who are not familiar with " The House of David," and to those who have a liking for Bible His- tory, we can strongly recommend the volume as being impressively and sympathetically written, and likely to prove interesting to a wide circle of readers. From Messrs. Cassell and Co., we have part 1 of "European pictures of the Year,"which is the companion work to " Royal Academy Pictures." In can be had in three parts, price Is. each ; or handsomely bound in one volume for 53. The pictures are reprcduced from the paintings of B Igium, Dutch, Russian and French artists of the year, and are printed and finished in a manner that lea VE3 nothing to be desired. A critical and des- criptive note on them, written by Mr. M. H. Spielman°, editor of" The Magazine of Art," will be issued with Part 111.

With this month (Nov.) " The Magazine of Art " com- mences a new volume, and for the future will contain three plates of the highest order of artistic merit which can be attained—alike in execution and in printing. These will consist of a Photogravure or an Etching as frontispiece, and two other plates, sometimes printed in colour, in order to heighten effect and give an added brilliancy to the pages of the magazine. They will be executed by the best processes of the day—either wood engraving, typogravure, or other method. The price of it will henceforth be Is. 4d. monthly, in order that the full intentions of the publishers may be adequately carried out, and judging from the three plates given with the Nov. number, the principal of which is an original etching, "The Alhambra," by H. Macbeth Raeburn, we have no doubt whatever that " The Magazine of Art" will be as valuable in the future as it has been in the past. Anther first part of a new, edition, is " The Family Ph .sician," a manual of domestic medicine by physi- cians and surgeons of the principal London hospitals. A wall sheet is included and priuted separately, entitled " The Family Physician Remembrancer," and is full of medical, surgical," and sanitary hints for every-day use.

The first yearly volume of " Chums" is out in time for a Christmas present for " our boys." T'le price of it is 7s. 6J., ic is handsomely bound in clot.. and is replete with everything in the way of literature that boys like, such as interviews with famous cricketers.and athletes, thrilling adventures of Ulysses, scores Of inter- esting, general, technical, and natural history, and last One in charity "is the name of a new navel by the Rev. Silas H. Kocking. By "our girls" (shall we say?) this book will be welcomed and appreciated, and for ourselves we need have no fear that they will meet with anything objectionable in it, as it is written with a judi- cious and delicate hand, and in the autkor's best style. It is a book that ought to find a place in the home of every intelligent, reading family.

- " " The English Illustrated Magazine" for November is a specially good number. The frontispiece is a portrait of the late Surgeon-Major Parke ; being one of five por- traits which illustrate an admirable article on the prin- cipal members of the Union Relief Xxpedition written by Mr. Herbert Ward,entitled "Martyrs to a New Crusade. " Reminiscences of Balliol College " by Mr. Andrew Lang, with illustrations by Holland Tringham,and " The shooting season at Sandringham" illustrated by the same artist, who represents H.R.U. The Prince of Wales ia a variety of shooting attitudes ; are both extremely inter- esting contributions. A Ramble through Shropshire" is charmingly pictured by Herbert Ronlon, a Blackburn artist, and " The story of a Mazurka " is a cleverly written complete story.

One of the most daintily bound books we have seen for a long time is " The City of Ilamilton," a souvenir 'plume which we have great pleasure in accepting frim the Mayor and Corporation of Hamilton—the Bir- mingham of Canada—a city of 50,000 inhabitants, sit uated at the wes• ern end of Lake Ontario. We cannot refrain from quoting the first paragraph of the introduc- tion, which says :—" Is the month of August, 1889, the City of Hamilton devoted' a week to holding a Grand Carnival. By an accidental missing of a train at Niagara Falls for New York, a party of English gentlemen who had been on a tlur through Canada and the United St itea, were induced to take the run of forty miles from Ni. g Ira to Hamilton, to kill time while awaiting the dep. r ure of the next train going east. So much struck were they with the city, its posi- tion, its beauty and resources, that what was intended to be a visit of a few hours be- came several weeks, and, on their arrival back in England, they wrote to the secretary of the Hamilton fl rd of Trade, informing him of the circumstances above recorded, and added "Of all the places we had visited during our trip on the American Continent, the prettiest, cleanest, healthiest, and hest conducted, was the city of Hamilton, Canada ; and from our inspection of the vast and varied manufacturing industries, its one hundred and seventy factories, with its 14,000 artisans, the large capital invested, and the immense output annually, we concluded it was well-named the Birming- ham of Canada, and has undoubtedly a great and glori- ous future before it." The letter finished with the query? "If we saw it by the accidental missing of a train, why not do something to call the attention of the outside world, so that people can go to your city and see for themselves its advantages ?' That letter has had much to dolwith the pubtishing of this Souvenir. The in- terior of the book—the letter press as well as the numer- ous and varied illustrations—is as daintily and perfectly finished as the exterior, and reflects great credit on the publishers—The Times Printing Co.—Hamilton.

Of all the quaintly interesting reproductions we have seen for same time, " Blaeu's Map of Lancashire," as it was in 1662, is the most so, and is very suggestive of the old prints given us with each issue of " The Picture Magazine." The map has been reproduced in the origi- nal size ; the towns, the villages, country houses, churches, mills, rivers, &c., with their old spellings, are all shown as they were known at that time; the pub- lishers are B. S. Shearer and Son, Stirling, N.B. The Christmas number of Mr. Stead's" Review of Reviews "is, as might be expected, a thoroughly ori- ginal production. 'the front of the cover contains a remarkably exact imitation of a schoolboy's slate with figures written upon it indicating that" Two and Two make Four,"and this, in fact, is the title of the number. It is, in the stri:dest sense, " A Story of the Times," as it is based upon the Liberator crash, and the characters introduced include, under very transparent disguises, the famous, or infamous, Jabez Balfour, and some of his accomplices. Mr. Stead himself also figures prominently under the pseudonym of Jasper Sterliog,as the conductor of a new "Daily Paper "which is to accomplish wonder ful things. A sample copy of the proposed new paper aceompanies the magazine, and from this it is to be seen that the paper will contain many original features both in its " get up " generally and in the compilation of its contents. But before bringing out this journal Mr. Stead asks that 100,000 people should send him a sovereign each, together with a year's subscription for the " Daily Paper," so that at one stroke he will secure the capital to finance his new venture and an assured circulation. Under such a scheme the readers will, of course, bethe shareholders, but Mr. Stead lays down the condition that he must have absolute control .as editor. It is a unique proposal, but will Mr. Stead get his £100,000?

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDA V. NOVEMBER 18, 1893.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA V. NOVEMBER 18, 1893.
NOTES .ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

Warrington added another victory to their account on Saturday, the victims this time being Barrow. They are new the fourth on the list in the league competition, so that they have every reason'to be on good terms with themselyes, considering the indifferent start they made. The viotory on Saturday was not such a fore- gone conclusion as the positions of the two clubs in the table would seem to indicate, because of late the Barrow club had been on the improving grade. The week that Warrington were receiving such a " slating" at the hands of Oldham, the Barrow men were entertaining the Wiganers who headed the league, and actually drew with them. Not content with that, the next week they had a trip to Oldham, and despite the fact that they had to play before the very one-sided Oldham spectators they were only beatcn by the narrow margin of a try,

With all these things to consider it was a very credit- able victory for Warrington on Saturday. That they were the best team on the field no one can deny. Their passing tactics were not as perfect as Barrow, but in everything else such as speed, tackling, and scrimmag- ing, they were superior.

On the Barrow side, T. Bowker was a very dangerous customer, owing to his nimble feet, as also WAS Dicken- son. Marshall and Chapman were also brilliant, but they bad the misfortune to find the two Bates in their best form which put them considerably into shade. The Barrow forwards were not so good as the Warrington forwardi, among whom Jolley was in brilliant form,and was very prominent during the whole of the game. Taylor another of the forwards also put himself very much en evidence besides being an excellent " shover."

As I said before, "Smack " and "Jack " Bate were in the best of form, and the try which they both shared in was an eye-opener for the Barrovians. Among the three-quarters Evans and Potts showed up the best. Webster was too closely watched to be able to display his abilities very much. Heesom played a most fearless g.nae, and he proved a great success as full back. The game was a most enjoyable one, and accidents were conspicuous by tneir absence, which was somewhat of a contrast to the Salford match.

The result of the competition stands thus : Phi. Won. Lost. Drn. UT. G.T. Pte. For. Agst. Swinton . 5 . 0 . 2 811 .. 1...12 Oldham 7 . 5.. 1 I . 11 11... 2 Win . 4 . 1 . 2 . 3 6 ... 1 0 —lO Warrington Tyldesley Salford Broughton dangers— 6 ... 2 ... 3 ... 1 ... 5 1 ... 4 6 ... 5 Rochdsle Hornets Barrow Broughton 6 . 0 . 6 . 0 . 1 2 ...18 13 ... 0

I notice that Ef. Webster had made his last appear- ance in Warrington ranks for some time at least. As last Saturday was only his second appearance this season, he has not had much chance of showing his form, lie is going to the Emerald Isle, and he will no doubt astonish the natives over there. The departure of such a jolly good fellow as Webster will be regretted by a wide circle of friends.

Warrington have now a rest for a fortnight from their work of climbing up the league ladder. To-day they meet the redoubtable Blackley team who are in the second league, and who have the splendid record of played 7, won 0, lost?, drawn 0, 0 points. If Warring- ton have their full team,they have a chance of making a record score. A good " gate " should be obtained to see whether this is the case or not.

I am pleased to note that in the Lancashire County match to be played at Workington, to-day (Saturday) when Lancashire will meet Cumberland, that two War- ington players have been selected to play for the county palatine. These are James T. Bate, and J. Jolley, who will no doubt do credit to the Warrington team. Among the reserve men I notice the name of John T. Bate, the captain of the local team, and his many ad- mirers would no doubt be glad to see him donning the county jersey. It will be remembered that in the match between the Whites v. Stripes he had the misfortune to be injured early in the match. Another feature in the Lancashire team is that the two half backs selected Bate and Chapman, were opposed to each other on the Warrington ground last Saturday in the Warrington v. Barrow match.

Westmoreland and Cheshire tried conclusions on Thurs day, at Kendal. Cheshire were without the assistance of Houghton, Abrahams, Davies, and Crompton, and were consequently considerably weakened. Play was of a very fast nature, and was rendered difficult by the half gale of wind which was sweeping the ground. At half time no scorn had been recorded, but during the second half Cheshire were. able to score three minors, whilst Westmorland were minus any such magic record.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AT WA R RINGTON.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AT WA R RINGTON.

As the completion ot the ,hip tiaflal wora uraws uear in this neighbourhood, the interest taken in the great venture by the public increases. During Saturday and Sunday last, the rumour that the flooding of the cutting would be commenced attracted hundreds of people to view the work at Latchford and Stockton Heath. It was seen then however, that the water could not be admit- ted for some days longer, because in several places the channel.was still encumbered with mechanical property. Other causes were al.o responsible for this. The flood- ing will be done chiefly from the Runcorn section and as the prevailing tides on the river are very low, it would be impossible to flood the nine miles of channel between Latchford and Runcorn, without drawing much of the water from the section already filled which is drained off at the Thelwall lacks. The engineers decided to wait therefore until the tides came sufficiently high to fill with ona or two floods, the required 28 feet of of water in the cutting. The mechanical arrangements for flooding are already complete. One foot below water level a wooden shoot has been run through the wall of earth which divides the lull channel from the empty. Within the shoot is a door, by means of which I the outflow may be carefully regulated. To break the fall of the water and save the bed of the channel what is technically known as a timber "apron' has been placed in position. By this contrivance the water is I diverted as over a sloping platform, and is carried for- ward without any violent rush. The same sluice ar- rangements are made at Randle's Creek, two and a half miles beyond Runcorn, a connection being in this way established direct with the Mersey when at flood height. Quite an army of men have been engaged during the week at Acton Grange finishing off the sides and charing the plant and working materials. A few yards from Acton Grange Bridge a wharfage is being constructed by Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., of the Haydock Col- lieries, to enable them to discharge their own railway coal trains direct into the sea-going vessels on the canal. For this purpose they contemplate laying down railway connection from Bank Quay Station.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT AC CON GRANGE.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT AC CON GRANGE.

On Thursday evening a train left the Old Quay at Run- corn, conveying a number of men to Latchford. When the train was descending the incline at Acton Orange,the couplings of the last waggon broke, and in response to the shouts of the men the driver stopped the train. The detached wagon continued its downward course with considerable speed, and dashed into the stationary train. Most of the occupants of the wagon were thrown out by the force of the concussion, and several sustained injuries to the limbs and legs, while others were severely shaken. The majority, however, proceeded to their work and the others were taken back to Runcorn. Rurr.ours of a most alarming kind were current in Run- corn, but happily proved untrue.

div.head: 1017NG WOMEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIA.TION.
div.p: THE 1017NG WOMEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIA.TION.

We have received from the Londen Young Women's Christian Association a copy of their last report which gives interesting details concerning the extensive and valuable work carried on by this Society. The associa- tion has in London about 40 institutes, hemes, and restaurants, 100 other branches, and two gymnasiums. In addition to the bible classes, evening educational classes, lectures,social evenings,&c.,are carried on at the various institutes. There are a number of departments designed to meet the special need of girls. These include employment agencies, saving bank and benefit club, , convalescent, sick aid and holiday fund, emigration, cir- cu'ating libraries, kn. The •• Travellers Aid Society" for the protection of girls when travelling, and the " Factory Helpers Union " which carries on work amongst factory girls, are under the auspices of the London Y.W.C.a. The membership numbers over 14,000 including all classes of girls, and there are more than 2.000 workers, mostly voluntary. The hon. Emily Kinnaird and Miss Morley are the hon. secretaries.

Mr. T. P. Lewis, M.P. for Anglegey, who has noti- fied to the local Liberal committee that he will not seek re-election owing to ill-health, is a septuage- narian. He is a tall, gaunt,melancholy-looking man of a taciturn turn of mind. lie prefers Welsh to English ;in fact, throughout his candidature he addressed all his meetings in Welsh. He is a deacon in the Calvinistic Methodist denomination, and a strong advocate of temperance. By trade he is a flour merchant, and Final his election as an M.P. has often sold bread over the counter of his shop in Bangor. Mr. Chamberlain arri4ed at Liverpool on Wednesday, on his return from the United States. He proceeded to London.

div.head: DisTßEss IN WAHRINGroN.
div.p: DisTßEss IN WAHRINGroN.

The subscriptions to the relief committee harp came in very plentifully this week in response to the appeal to people outside ‘Varrington made by the Committee last week. There has been over £4OO received independent of local subscriptions. This will relieve the Committee considerably and they have now good hopes of tiding over the dispute in the coal trade. Mr. Hartley, the preberve manufac- turer, Aintree, has maftle the mugnificent gift of three and a half tons of preserve of the value of £5O. This is the second time that Mr. Hartley has shown his generosity since the relief committee com- menced its labours. Messrs. Richardson have also given a waggon load of coal which is being distri- buted by the Ladies Committee. With regard to the works there is very little change to report. The steel furnace at Houghton's Sankey Wire Mills has u work again, and work has been partially ocg recommenCed at Monks, Hall and Cos'. this week, but there will probably be but slight change until the miners recommence work.

RELIEF COMMI CTEE'S WEEKLY MEETING. LARGE INCREASE OF SUBSCRIPTIONS. The weekly meeting of the Relief Committee, was held yesterday, in the Council Chamber, of the Town Hall. Mr. Stanley Wilson, announced that the Mayor would not be able to be presenc at the meeting owing to his being unwell. The Mayoras would also not be pre- sent, and Mr. Monks had an important engagement in Manchester, which would prevent his attendance at the meeting. Mr. Edelsten was elected chairman on the motion of the Rev. Owen Watkins seconded by the Rev. W. H. Drummond. The Chairman then gave the weekly statement. During the week there had been 23,840 pints ot soup distributed, against 25,012 last week ; 26,502 lbs. of bread against 29,029 ; and the tea and sugar had been much the same. The expenditure had been £lB7 ss. 2d., against £lB7 11s. 91. last week. The expenditure had thus been practically the same although the distribution had been less. This was ex- plained by the fact that there had been fewer gifts of provisions and everything had had to be bought. The local subscriptions received last week had amounted to £l4B, an average amount. The result of the appeal sent to the "Times" and other London, Liverpool, and Manchester papers had been very satis- factory. By that morning they bad received £430 17s. Bd. (Applause.) This made the total subscriptions since the commencement of £2,134 2s. 4d. W hich left a balance on the ordinary fund of £lB3 14s. 7d. besides which the outside subscriptions were also available. The executive committee felt justified in recommending an extension of the charity, which would consist of giving an extra oz. of tea to the families of six and over, and also a pot of jam to be given to each family. He might mention that Mr. Hartley had given 3i tons of jam. (Applause.) It would enable them to give a pot of jam to each family, and possibly there would be some jam to spare. Another recommendation of the committee was that people receiving relief might receive coal from the coal dealers at the ordinary prices of 9d. or 10d. per cwt., and the balance would be paid by the relief committee. Eight tons of coal had also been received from Messrs. Vs. J. Richardson, which was being distributed by the ladies' committee in cases of sickness. A large I amount of clothing had been received during the week, the Council Chamber being almost full, and ' some of the things were almost as good as new. These also were being distributed by the ladies committee. A letter had been received from the Volunteers with respect to the Drill Hall, which was as follows signed by Major Ridgway ;—" As you are aware we are not charging anything for the use of the Drill Hall. lam glad of this opportunity to say on behalf of the committee (Finance Committee), that this affords them extreme pleasure to be able to contri- bute the use of the room for so wmthy, though so melancholy an object. You will however give pub- licity te the fact that the Drill Hall is the private pro- perty of the volunteers, not a public room. This would relieve us of trouble in future applications." As a volunteer officer, he (the chairman) would say that it was a great plea.ure to the officers to put the room at the disposal of the committee. At the same time it would be unfortunate if the impression prevailed that the Drill Hall was not a public room which might be had at any time. If this impression prevailed it would lead to embarrassment.

The Rev. Owen Watkins moved that in future one lb of sugar and two ozs. of tea to be given to families of over six, and also a pot of jam to every family on Saturday. The Rev. John Yonge seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. The Rev. W. H. Drummond moved that arrange, merits be made whereby coal might be purchased at the normal prices, the extra charge to be found by the ex- ecutive committee. The executive committee did not intend to put this into force the present week, but ar- rangements would be made during the coming week. The motion was seconded,but before it wavut,the fb-v E. 'r. Reed said that there were persons who would be unable even to pay 9d. He hoped that some distinction would be made between those families in which so me of the members were working, and those in which there were none.
The Rev. W. H. Drummond said that as there were 1,600 families relieved, it would be an immense difficulty to discriminate. The Ladies' Committee, however,eould relieve the more needy cases.

The Rev. Owen Watkins thought that the Committee should express their greatest thankfulness and gratitude at the way in which their friends in different parts of the country had so nobly responded to the appeal made last week. He would include Mr. Hartley and Messrs. Richardson, the friends from Southport and elsewhere. The Rev. E. C. E Carleton seconded the resolution, and said that he hoped the resolution would find its way into the provincial press.
'the Chairman in supporting the resolution, said that the Committee had received subscriptions not only from different parts of England but also from Ireland and Paris.
The resolution was carried unanimously.

The Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis), proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Gladstone for his action in bringing the coalowners and miners together. The Rev. J. Yonge seconded the motion. He thought that the Rector /IA very happily taken this opportunity. It would be a graceful act to pass the resolution before the result was known.
_ The Chairman _ supported and the resolution was passed unanimously. _ • _
BANKEY BRIDGES.

The numbers who have been provided with free teas at the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel, during the past week have been Saturday, 160 men ; Tuesday, 380 chil- dren ; Wednesday, 212 women; Thursday, 425 children. ' During the week, Mrs. Cooke and other Penketh friends had sent a quantity of clothing to be di,tributed among the children. In addition to this they had sent £2,P id- gate friends £1 16.3., and a friend £5. The Appleton Wesleyans-also collected £1 16s. on Sunday for the same object. On Saturday night an entertainment was given in the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel, the whole ar- rangements being in the hands of the young men of Pen- keth. The Chairman was Mr. C. E. Parker, and in the course of his speech he said that he was glad that the men were bearing up in their distress so bravely and pluckily. He alluded to the high price of coal which would have a tendency to driving away the trade of this country. He hoped that this consideration would have its weight with the masters and men in their de- liberations. With regard to the relief in Sankey Bridges, he said that they had nothing to fear as, until the end of the coal dispute, the Penketh friends would bear half the expenses. The following programme was then gone through :—Pianoforte solo, Mrs. Parker ; recitation, " Football Bob," Mr. Donovan ; accordian solo, " Ye hamks and braes," Mr. Picton ; La ncashme sketch, Mr. Davies ; flute solo, " Variations of Scotch airs," Mr. Seed ;trio, " Torpedo and the whale," Messrs. J. Smith, J. Seed, and T. Villkinson ; reading, "Curtain lecture," Mr. B. Cooke; glee," Let the hills resound," the Penketh ' glee party ; accordian solo, " Annie Laurie," Mr. Picton; , song, " New kingdom," Miss Routledge ; dialogue, " Bachelor's wants," Messrs Smith, Seed,Davies, Wilkin- son, and Sudden ; song, Mr. Sudden ; recitation, " Billy's rose," Mr. Philip Garnett ; glee, " Softly flow the shadesof evening," the glee party.—.A vote of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Mr. J. Summersgill, seconded by Mr. W. Brough, brought an interesting gathering to a close. MEETING OF IRONWORKERS.

We have been supplied with the following report : At a largely attended meeting of ironworkers held in Bewsey forge on Tuesday, after considerable discussion which was joined in by most of the leading hands includ- ing Messrs. Councillor Beaman, Thomas Chadwick, T. Malkin, James Rudge, George Urmston, Joseph Bunch, John Budge and others, the following resolution was passed unanimously :—" That this meeting of ironwork- ers calls upon the mineowlters and miners to at once sub. mit their dispute to arbitration, the colliers to begin work at once pending the decision." The resolution was forthwith forwarded to the mineowners and miners respective federations."

At the usual monthly meeting of the Watch Commit tee of the St. Helens Corporation on Wednesday, the reports of Chief Constable Wood and of Fire-Superinten- dent Rutherford on the recent fire at ttie Greenbank Works of the United Alkali Company were read. In connection with the fire there were several exceptional circumstances. The superintendent was driving the steam fire-engine round the corner of Hardshaw-st. and Church-st., when the hind wheel caught the kerb, and was smashed. The engine had to be left, and the manual fetched, on which the half-a-dozen firemen, who had been thrown off the engine, were coeveved to the fire. One man, named Seddon, had his ankle dislocated and thigh bone injured. A further deterrent circum- stance was that for some time water could not be raised to the great elevation of the burning vitriol chambers, and the hose belonging to the Corporation was damaged by the escaping vitriol. The committee, after consider- leg the reports, appointed a sub-committee to consider the whole matter, with a view to the thorough reonaut, sation of the fire thigade,

RE-OPENING OF PITS. A &putition representing TyWesley miners having waited upon Messrs. W. Ramsden and Sons to see if an arrangement could be come to, it was decided to open the pits at the .11c1 rate. This makes the third firm in the divishon which has re-opened at the old rate this week.

A meeting was held on Wednesday at the Griffin Hotel, Eccleston, of the men belonging to the Eccleston Hall Colliery, to consider an offer from the owners (Messrs. Worsley, Mesnes, and Co). The meeting was presided over by Mr. T. Stephenson, check weigliman. Mr. T. Greenall, miners' agent, Pendlebury, was present. A deputation was appointed to wait on the manager at the colliery. 'The result was that the men aro to return to work at once at the old rate, each man to have his own place of working. About 150 will be put on. The bulk of them reside at Prescot, where great satisfaction is manifested at the result. iS Staited that the men on strike at the Chapelhouse Colliery, Skelmersdal;, numbering over 400, returned to work on Wednesday morning at the old rate of wages.

HARD TREATMENT OF YORKSHIRE DEPUTIES. A Pontefract correspondent telegraphs :—Two Nostell deputies had ejectment order issued against them on Wednesday to quit the houses they occupy under Lord St. Oswaicl, and five others are to be applied for on Sat- urday. One of the deputies was interviewed by a reporter, and said that they worked six weeks after the stoppage commenced, but were so menaced and roughly handled by mobs that they stayed away a week. On returning they were ordered to get coal for the firm's use, but they dared not. They were then dismissed, and ordered out of the colliery dwelling. HAYDOCK.—MR. S. WOODS, M.P., AND MR. GRIMKE-DRAY CON.

Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for Newton Division, which includes Haydock, has given notice that he will put the following question in the House of Commons on Monday next :—" To ask the Secretary of State fonsthe Home Department if he has received from the managing direc- tor of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Haydock, Lan- cashire, a copy of a letter addressed to him by Mr. S. Woods, M.P., miner's agent, complaining that the firm had induced men to resume work at their Go!borne col- lieries, stating that the men so employed were running a great risk, and wanting the firm to discontinue work ; and also stating that he (Mr. Woods) contemplated hold- ing a mass meeting at one of the collieries in question in order to protest against the continuance of work ? Whether subsequet t to the publication of the letter a brutal assault was committed at Golborne upon one of the men who had been so employed, and if it is intended to secure protection from outrage and intimidation to men willing to work. MR. JUSTICE DAY ON THE RIOTING AT HAYDOCK. _ _

Mr. Justice Day, addressing the grand jury at Liver- pool Assizes on Wednesday, said they would have to investigate the charge against fifteen persons of rioting in the neigbonrhood of the colliery at Haydock. Rioting was a very grave offence. It tended to disturb law and order, and consequently disturbed the foundations of civilisation and society. If men were ta be at liberty to enforce their own will upon others,and to defy the law, and its officers, it would put an end to civilisation and bring ruin and disaster not only upon people who had money, but still greater disaster upon those who had no money, but who sought to make available their industry for money. Anything that tended to disturb law and order tended to injure the poor a great deal more than the rich. Capital might be readily removed: to other places. Labour was not so easily removed, and if linen would hut consider the ruin their conduct was too often calculated to entail upon their fellows, they would be less disposed to take part in suet] outrages, and more inclined to observe those rules of order which were essen- tial to the welfare and prosperity of everyone, whatever his rank in life. It was absolutely necessary that per- eons guilty of rioting should be brought to justice, and this in the interests of every class of the community.

div.head: GOVERNMENT MEDIATION.
div.p: GOVERNMENT MEDIATION.
The following letter was addressed on Monday by Mr. Gladstone to the Federations •of owners and miners :

"Sr,—The attention of Her Majesty's Government has been seriously called to the widespread and disast- rous effects produced by the long continuance of the un- fortunate dispute in the coal trade, which has now en- I tered upon its sixteenth week. It is clear from inform- ation which has reached the Board of Trade tpat much misery and suffering are caused not only to families of, the men directly involved, bu also to many thousands of others not engaged in mining whose em- ployment has been adversely affected by the stoppage. , The further prolongation of the dispu r cannot fail to aggravate this suffering, especially in view of the apv...,,a. ut n lutes, flhieU UC, I Cfl.ll, lLsl.lrL.fla pi ILe tie fuel is likely to cause distress among the poorer classes throughout the country. Moreover,the Government have little doubt that the effect of the stoppage en industry is rapidly extending and increasing,and that,unless an early settlement is effected, lasting, if not permanent, injury may be done to the trade of the country. The Govern- ment have not up to the present considered that they advantageously intervene in a dispute the settlement ef which would far more usefully be brought about by the action of those concerned in it than by the good offices of others ;but having regard to the serious state of affairs referred to above, to the national importance of a speedy termination of the dispute, and to the fact that the conferences which took place on the 3id and 4th of November did not result in a settlement, Her Majesty's Government have felt it their duty to make an effort to bring about a resumption of negotiations between the employers and employed under conditions-svhich may lead to a satisfactorytresult. It appears to them that advantage might accrue from a further discussion be- tween the parties of the present position of matters, under the chairmanship of a member of the Government who, it is hoped, will not be unacceptable to either side.

"Lord Rbsebery has consented, at the request of his colleagues, to undertake the important duty which Such a position involves. I have therefore to invite the Miners' and the Coalowners' Federations to send repre- sentatives to a conference to be held forthwith un&r his chairmanship. "In discharging this duty it is not proposed that, Lord Rosehery should assume the position of an arbitrator or umpire, or hims2lf vote on the proceedings, but that he should confine his action to offering his good offices in erder to assist the parties in arriving at a friendly settle- ment Qf the qv/56°n in dispute—lam, Sm.,
W. E. GLAD. sToNE,."

THE CONFERENCE. The joint conference of delegates representing the coal- owners and miners was held yesterday (Friday) at the Foreign Office, Lord Rosebery presiding; and there is at last hope .f settlement of the coal trade dispute, especi- ally as it is stated that both sides have an earnest desire to terminate the struggle. On Thursday the coalowners selected their delegates ; and the representatives chosen by the miters left their districts for London on Thursday night. Mr. L. Smith of the Labour Department of the Board of Trade, will act as secretary to the conference. Mr. S. Woods, M.P. speaking at Wigan on Wednesday night, oftid if the colliery proprietors would give the men seven shillings per day and a guarantee that the rate of payment should go no lower than this living wage the men were quite willing that their wages should be regulated by arbitration, conciliation hoard, or sliding scale.

The selection of delegates from the masters' side oc- cupied the committee of the Coalowners' Association two hours and a half on Thursday. Messrs. Alfred Hewlett, John Knowles, and Richard Pilkington, along with Mr. Ratcliffe Ellis, the general secretary to the as- sociation, are the Lanea.thire and Cheshire delegates ; Mr. A. div.head: ALARMING PIT ACCIDENT IN SCOTLAND.
div.p: ALARMING PIT ACCIDENT IN SCOTLAND.

A rather alarming fire occurred at the Kirkwood col- liery of the Summerlee and Mossend Iron and Steel Com- pany at Coatbridge on Thursday evening. By the up- setting of a paraffin lamp at the pithead the framework was burned down, and all means of communication with the men below, 42 in untidier was cut off. It was for a time feared that all hope of saving the men was gone; but late on Thursday night a volunteer party descended the shaft to explore, and word was ultimately sent to to the top that all the entombed min.rs were safe—an announcement which was greeted with loud cheering by he anxious relatives and friends at the pit mouth.
