div.head: FOREIGN MHSIONARY ANNIVERSARY AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH.
div.p: FOREIGN MHSIONARY ANNIVERSARY AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH.

At Wycliffe Church on Sunday,sermous were preached on behalf of the London Missionary Society. The pulpit at the morning service was occupied by the Rev. Owen Watkins, Wesleyan minister, and lately missionary in &nth Africa. Mr. Watkins said his presence in that pulpit was evidence of the close brotherhood that existed between the Wesleyans and the London Missionary So- ciety. As most of them were aware, he was an African missionary, and had given seventeen years and the best of his life to work in Central Africa. He believed a man couldn't be a Christian unless he had a missionary spirit. Mr. Watkins mentioned the good work done by Robert Moffatt in Atrica, and as he (Mr. Watkins) went over Warrington bridge he felt he was on holy ground, for it was on Warrington, bridge that Robert Moffatt saw a bill announcing a missionary meeting at Manchester, which led him to change his life, and enter the service of the London Missionary Society. Mr. Watkins afterwards gave a vivid account of his own experiences in Africa, and the success of Christianity in that land. An address to the Sunday school scholars was given in the after- noon by Captain Hore, returned missionary from Lake Tanganika, who also preached at the evening service. He tee;; for his text "There remaineth yet very much land to be poa.,,:vssed," Joshua 13c. lv. In an earnest missionary sermotl in Whicii the preacher gave his ex- periences in missionary work for eleven years,he nfuted the statement maab by Mr. •H. M. Stanley that the Afri- cans herded together h. ke ammals,and said that they lived in families, and were as warlike as. represented. Collections were taken at , each service in aid of the funds of the London Mission. %ry Society. Special an- thems were sung by the choir, toder the conductorship of Mr. G. Wallington.

div.head: TB E P.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE aIIJECII.
div.p: TB E P.S.A. AT WYCLIFFE aIIJECII.

- - •• - -- The usual P.S.A. meeting in Wycliffe Ght.xych on Sun, day afternoon was largely attended, and thd Member- ship still increases. Mr, John Porritt was the chali.man, and in the course of a short address, he said that he never knew a religious movement, which met the wants of workingmen better than the P.S.A. movement. As a Sunday school worker for 35 years, he knew that in the Sunday school they were met with the difficult pro- blem of hcw to retain their elder scholars' but he con- sidered that the P.S.A. movement had solved that pro- blem. There was an immense amount of work in con- nection with that movement, which found work for the young men who had left the Sunday school, and thus kept them from drifting from it. The Rev. J. W. Varley was the speaker for the afternoon, and addressed those present on their right as men to be men, and to be 11 treated as men. Two solos were well rendered by Mr. A. Griffiths and Mrs. J. W. Varley. The meeting was also taken part in by Mr. T. Wallington and Mr. R. Atkinson.

div.head: REV, J. W. VARLEY AND THE DRINK TRAFFIC.
div.p: THE REV, J. W. VARLEY AND THE DRINK TRAFFIC.

At the Baptist Chapel, Wash-lane, Latchford, on Sun- day night, the Rev. J. W. Varley took as the subject of his discourse "Three wars—the Matabele war, the coal war, the drink war," The rev. gentleman took as his text Proverbs 14-34. He pointed out that it was the duty of ministers in regard to the moral and social questions of the day, to trinuld and lead the opinions of their congregations, and not to wait for them or follow them. Coining to the Matabele war, he said that there were two principles which ought to guide them in dis- cussing this question, as- also the coal war, and the drink war. Firstaivery war should be undertaken in self- defence. No war was justifiable which started out to filch a neighbour's property, or to take advantage of human nature. Secondly, a war 'should be undertaken in a righteous cause. Mr. Vexley then briefly reviewed the circumstances which led up to the Matabele war, dealing with the Budd concession by Lobengula, and showed frem quotations from different despatches, and from the testimony of Lord Kuutsford and the Colonial Office that the concession was gained under the grossest deception,to which he added the testimony of Lobengula himself. He pointed out that the Matabele war was en• tered upon with the sole desire to filch rand in order to dig for minerals. Dealing with the ceal war, he urged that it was no ordinary conflict between capital and labour, but a strife in which the whole question of the ownership of the mineral was involved. He quoted from Mr. Proud° and the "Daily Chronicle," to show that in no civilized country save England, did the owner- ship of the surface convey with it abseltate and uncon- ditional ownership of the minerals beneath. He went on to speak strongly upon the rights of property being exaggerated over the rights of the persen, The coal war was really a war for the right to existsveluth claimed consideration for the living man, as well as For the coal dividend, and claimed for him to have a fair and reason- able amount of God's fresh air for some parts of the week. In coming to the question of the drink In War- rington. he said that he had no desire tu exnggerate it evils, but he asked whether the gravity of the position was recognised. Had the citizens of the borough re- cognised the condition of things by which- they were surrounded? He alluded to a letter from the Rev. Thee. tesse, eivesiseae minister, in which that aetetlemee that since he had left Warrington, he had begun to realise some of the awful evils of the drink tralßC in the town. Look at the position of affairs in the town. /n the first place, he (Mr. Varley) noticed that there were two large breweries which threw their dark and dismal 'shadow over the whole of the borough. There were hundreds of people who were directly or indirectly bene- fitted by themfoney which lowed from the exchequer of of teese two breweries, and many men supported the breweries because of trading interests. In the town, there were 150 licensed houses, or one to about 350 people, and if the temperance portion of the population were taken away, there would be one public-house to every 250 people. The breweries had a great inflherree at municipal and general elections. He asked if beer and publicans did not play an important part in the af- fairs of the constituency ? He had been informed that something like 500 votes could be very easily bought in the town. He next dealt with the Town Council: He asked if they took away from the present Town Cbun- cil those who were publicans, distillers, and maltsters, and those who were connected be trade, or professional' work, or those who had been connected with the drink trade, how many would they have left ? He was very much inclined to say what was said of Sodom and Go- morrah, if affairs continued the same for a few years,. "There were not eve righteous left." He wished his hearers to look at the Watch Committee. The Chief Constable was well known to be an amiable and estim- able man, and one who desired to do his duty. He was almost bound hand and foot. It was well known that there was a large amount of betting and gambling-car- ried on in the town, but the Chief Constable could take no act len because he was not authorised to do so by hie superiors. He (Mr. Varley) pointed to Monday morn- ings at the Police Court,in which there was a large num- ber of eases, seven-eights of which were brought there through drink. He had been disgusted in listening at various times to the pious moralising of certain mem- ters of the Bench, who, in spite of the fact that the-men came many of them through drink, were yet thick and thin supporters of this trade in the town. What, he asked, were the Christian people of the town going to do in the face of these things, for it was to the Chris- tian portion of the population that these things must ultimately be referred ? He did not think that only teetotalers should engage in time war, but everyone who desired the betterment of the town in which he lived should join in the ranks. What had been done in North Toxteth, Liverpool, could to some extent be dDee in Warrington. Thirty years ago it was determined that no building land should be given unless the owners prohi- hit-d the sale of intoxicating liquors on the premises. This had kept licensed houses out of a district of 168 streets, 10,000 houses, and 50,000 people. This district is the best tenanted in tee city. There were only 45 people receiving relief in this district, and the poor Tate was only 10d. This was in striking contrast with an adjoining district in which there was a large number of public-houses. Before they could get to this admirable state of things in Warrington, there were two or three considerations to be looked at. The entire destruction of public-houses he believed was impossible, because public opinion was against such action ; perhaps it was thought to be too harsh treatment of abusiness, and it was thought necessary to have a few for the convenience of some people. Those who wished for reforms must abandon theory anti adopt practice. Not to- work was to be criminal. Everyone, whether Tory or Liberal, Churchman or Nonconformist, men with a creed or no creed, should do their utmost to bring about higher morals, and join in this most important wowk.

The Countess Kearney, who has been heard at several political meetings in Glasgow within the past year, is a daughter of the late Colonel Percival, and granddaugh- ter of Sir William Palmer, of Kenure Park, Dublin. Wiekere, were charged with stealing a cwt. of coal from the works of Messrs. Ankers and Son.
